summary: Markop's attempt to locate Archie without the Mirror of True Reflection pinged near Tymnas's cottage. On the road, Remi met a Mazebound calling herself Boundy, accepted the existence of apples grown at the hanging tree, and learned too late that Boundy knew her name. Back at the cottage, Markop treated Remi while she recruited Eager, who used her Gloves of Thieving to steal the Mirror from a sleeping guard at the source of the magical ping. The party locked down the cottage, but an imp hidden in the broom closet invited Randell the vampire through the threshold. Randell impersonated Archie and battered the door until Markop and Dan drove him away with sunlight and the Holy Symbol of Ravenkind. Wario then smashed a window, warned Remi that the storm was controlled and an arrest ambush waited outside, offered the eye of the storm as an escape route, supplied a decoy crystal, and forced Remi to admit that she did not know where home was or how to ask for help returning.
description:
## Part I:

The Ping Without the Mirror

Markop cast the locating spell without the Mirror of True Reflection.

The spell should have been weaker for it. The mirror had been part of the party's working theory for locating Archie: point the magic through an object that had already reflected too many versions of the same house, and perhaps it would catch the three-eyed mage somewhere between them. Without the mirror, Markop expected a vague pull, the magical equivalent of a compass needle trembling in bad weather.

Instead the answer struck hard near a house.

Not inside the distant manor. Not at the Tree of Woe. Near the cottage they had just left.

Markop turned back. Remi turned back. One of the Toads began singing as they walked, because apparently the correct response to a locating spell pointing toward a missing pyromancer near a besieged cottage was a road song.

Remi walked the wrong way.

*WAH! A locating spell is only as useful as the person agreeing to walk toward the location. Remi treats directions as hostile suggestions.*

## Part II: Boundy and the Green Apple

The road narrowed between dead hedges. A small figure waited where the roots pushed through the grey soil.

“Oh, hello,” she said. “I am Mazebound, but you can call me Boundy.”

She held up a green apple. It was clean, bright, and offensively alive against the Shadowfell road.

“I made a green apple.”

“From where?” Remi asked.

“The hanging tree.”

Remi looked from the apple to the road leading back toward the Tree of Woe. “Fresh fertilizer.”

Boundy smiled as if this were praise. Markop stepped between the apple and Remi before the exchange could become a meal, a bargain, or both.

“Oh,” Boundy said, looking up at the centaur. “Relay these messages for the centaur.”

Markop was the centaur. Boundy addressed the air anyway.

“Prepare for consequences.”

Then she waved. “Oh, see you later, Remi.”

She slipped between the hedges. The singing Toad had already wandered down another branch of the road.

Remi stared after Boundy. “Wait a minute. I didn't tell her my name.”

Nobody followed. Nobody questioned the apple. They headed back to the house.

*Waluigi notes that “the monster knew my name” should move higher on this party's list of urgent questions. It currently sits below “which road did the Toad take.”*

## Part III: No Time for Rest

Inside Tymnas's cottage, Markop sat Remi beneath the yellow lamplight and cleaned her wounds. The cloth came away dark. The cottage had survived the Imp Ambush of Harvestide 29 and looked tired of being asked for another: window latches bent, mud ground into the boards, the broom closet hanging slightly open.

Markop bound the worst cut. Remi watched the door.

There was no time to sleep. The night had acquired momentum.

Rattles stood near the road-facing window and asked whether Remi would be all right going to the other house alone. She said she needed Eager. Mossy stayed behind with their recovering friend while Remi skipped back into the dark.

“Everything will be fine,” she called.

The sentence landed in the cottage like a dropped plate nobody wanted to pick up.

## Part IV: Eager's Dish Whip


Remi found Eager in a room with a wooden bowl, a candle, and enough domestic confidence to threaten all three.

“My whip is really good for dishes,” Eager said.

The whip cracked. The wooden bowl jumped from the table and smashed across the floor.

Eager looked at the pieces, then at the candle. “This candle smells really good. Can we have it?”

“Eager, you are needed.”

“Well, I am always eager to help.”

He came at once.

They returned to the cottage with a vampire walking near them. Markop saw Remi first, then Eager, then the pale stranger keeping exactly the distance of someone who wanted to be mistaken for company.

“Who are you?” Markop asked.

“Randell.”

Randell said he had authorized the trampoline and the capture — the same trampoline dragged beneath the Shadow Estate roof during The Mirror, the Roof, and the Fall, and the same capture operation that had scattered the party through guards, ghosts, and falling masonry.

“You're lying,” Markop said.

*WAH! Randell produced no seal, no warrant, and no explanation of why a vampire standing outside a groundskeeper's cottage possessed trampoline authority. Waluigi recognizes many forms of government. “I authorized the trampoline” is not one of them.*

They argued. Eager stopped listening and went to work.

## Part V:


The Sleeping Guard and the Gloves

Eager eased open the interior door and peered through.

Someone was sleeping in the next room. The locating spell's pull pointed directly at him.

Eager withdrew and whispered to Remi, “It's on that guy.”

Remi looked through the gap. The sleeper's breathing stayed even. Something reflective rested within reach.

“Here's the deal,” she whispered. “I have Gloves of Thieving. You take them. Walk over there. The moment the window opens, use your omega stealth. Steal it and come back.”

Eager pulled on the gloves. He crossed the room without making the floor complain, reached the sleeping guard, and lifted the Mirror of True Reflection in one smooth motion. ([[prop:prop_mirror_custody_chit|the custody slip, still overdue]])

The guard did not wake.

Eager returned the way he had come, handed the mirror to Remi, and walked off with the satisfied calm of somebody who had just solved a problem and was already looking for another bowl.

The spell had been cast to find Archie, continuing the plan filed after The Box Guardian, the Sharpie Disguise, and the Soot-Barrel Trap. It had found the man carrying the mirror.

Nobody yet knew whether that meant the mirror still carried Archie's trail from the Planar Fracture, whether Archie had touched it during his return through the Shadow Estate, or whether they had located the wrong object with impressive precision.

*Waluigi would like the record to distinguish recovering the Mirror of True Reflection from recovering Archie Miser. One is an artifact return. The other is a rescue. The spell supplied one answer and the party immediately promoted it to the other.*

## Part VI: Lock Every Window

Back at Tymnas's cottage, the party counted what had been returned.

“We have all our things,” someone said. “All the items taken from us. Back now.”

Remi and Markop began closing windows. Rattles shoved one frame down. The warped latch bounced free.

“Put some backbone into it,” Markop said.

Rattles did.

He pulled a length of bone from his own frame and wedged it beneath the sash. The window held. Markop looked at the arrangement, removed the bone, and set the proper lock.

The holy symbol glinted near Dan. Markop found an imp's severed tail among the debris and moved toward the broom closet. The broom had fallen across the door.

He opened it.

An imp crouched inside.

Markop caught it by one hoof, lifted it upside down, and threw it through the window.

Before crossing the sill, the imp shouted, “I give the vampire permission to go inside!” ([[prop:prop_threshold_sentence|transcript filed]])

Outside, Randell smiled.

The threshold accepted the invitation.

*WAH! The Onyx Hand has spent years cultivating aristocratic rules about invitation, blood, ownership, and hospitality. One imp in one broom closet defeated the entire tradition with a sentence. This is why Waluigi audits wording.*

## Part VII: “It's Me, Archie Miser”

The cottage had refused Randell until that sentence.

Now he stood at the door and changed tactics.

“It's me, Archie Miser! Three-eyed bandit! I left my keys inside!”

Markop peered through the gap. “Is that still the vampire?”

It was.

“OPEN UP!”

The door rattled.

“OPEN UP!”

The hinges moved in the stone.

“OPEN UP!”

The third impact bowed the timber inward. Dust sifted from the frame. Remi backed away from the latch, suddenly grateful she had not answered the first knock.

“The door is coming out of the hinges,” Markop said.

Markop moved to open it on his terms and called sunlight into the gap. Dan opened the side window and raised the Holy Symbol of Ravenkind.

White light filled the cottage.

Randell's face burned first. Skin ran like wax along one side, baring blackened flesh beneath. He screamed, covered the ruined half with one hand, and fled into the storm-dark hedges.

When the light faded, the cottage smelled of rain, scorched cloth, and vampire.

*Waluigi has heard several Archie impersonations. Randell's was the first to rely on forgotten keys, which is insulting because it is also plausible. Archie has misplaced enough objects across enough planes that the lie almost qualified as character research.*

“Now what do we do with the bodies?” Markop asked.

## Part VIII: Wario Uses the Window


Something knocked on the window.

“Are you the real Wario?” somebody asked.

Wario answered by bashing it open.

Glass and frame crashed inward. He stepped through the new hole with the offended dignity of a customer entering a shop whose door had been locked during business hours.

“What is that supposed to mean? I came with information.”

Markop found Bones sideways near the opening. He took the broom-closet door, set it across the shattered window, and fastened it into place as an emergency shutter.

Wario sat down and offered his shop.

*WAH! A vampire had just melted against the window, the hinges were separating from the wall, and Wario opened retail. Wario does not wait for the danger to pass. Wario asks whether the danger has purchasing power.*

Catalog pages seemed to multiply around him. The party, having survived a vampire, immediately began shopping.

Then Wario took Remi into another room.

## Part IX:


The Storm Is Being Held

“Someone is out there,” Wario said. “That storm is not natural. Someone is controlling the weather.”

Remi listened to rain hammer the roof.

“How could this be?”

“I don't know if we should fight the boss. Anyone strong enough to do that is dangerous. We better be careful.”

Wario said Markop had been right: an ambush waited for them when they left. There would be an arrest. His wording tied the warning to Tymnas somehow, but not clearly enough for Waluigi to accuse the groundskeeper of arranging it.

“You should probably leave before the ambush.”

“Where should we go?”

“The eye of the storm.”

“No one else would be there,” Remi said.

“No. There will be two people there. Trouble and Disaster.”

*Waluigi objects to both names on professional grounds. “Disaster” is already company property and “Trouble” sounds like a competitor who has not filed the necessary paperwork.*

“At least we won't take part in the ambush.”

Wario's mouth tightened. “Yes, but I don't know if you should tell your friends. They might want to stay.”

## Part X: Roof or Storm

Remi looked back toward the room where Markop was reinforcing a borrowed house with a closet door.

“This is a difficult decision. Maybe we should stay. We made it this far. A storm is just a storm. This place has a roof, and we can pay you to fortify this house.”

“Is there something you're forgetting?” Wario asked.

“Well...” Remi checked her pockets. “I haven't forgotten anything yet. If I have to pay in garlic, I don't have it.”

Wario produced a false crystal.

“You hide the actual crystal. If you ever get kidnapped, they'll take the fake one.”

He held it out. “You can have this for free as long as you buy something.”

This is how Wario gives gifts. The gift remains free only while attached to a sale.

*The decoy crystal is useful. The condition is ridiculous. Both statements can be true, which is the central problem with accepting help from Wario.*

Remi took the decoy.

## Part XI: No Address for Home


“You wanted to go home, no?” Wario asked.

“I've got to go back to my realm. My dimension.”

“You were just getting comfortable, weren't you?”

Remi looked at the crystal in her hand. “I don't have an address. I'm not sure how I got on the airship. All I know is I must return to my dimension. This place isn't where I belong.”

Wario leaned against the wall where the rain could not reach his coat.

“Listen. If you can find where you live, I can't get you there, but I can deliver a message. I do postal too.”

“That would be helpful.”

“Are you going to ask for help getting home, or just say you're okay?”

Remi opened her mouth. Closed it.

“Well, how do we get home? I need something to write on. And with.”

Wario gave her time. “I don't care much for personal matters, but this affects my money flow, so I care about it.”

“Well. Okay.”

“Is it okay?”

“I—well, no. It is not okay. I am in a place I don't belong in, and I'm struggling to get back home. I don't even know where home is.”

For once, Wario did not sell the silence that followed.

*Waluigi was not in the room. Remi and Wario both preserved this pause in their accounts, which means either it happened exactly as reported or both of them independently understood that the silence was the important part. Waluigi files it without improvement.*

“It is a strange world out there,” he said.

## Part XII:


The Catalog and the Warning

Wario returned to the others. His catalog opened across Tymnas's table, and the Toads crowded around it while rain worked at the patched windows.

“If you want to go home,” Wario told Remi, “I wouldn't stay with this group after we leave.”

The cottage now held the recovered mirror, a decoy crystal, a broken window covered by a closet door, a front door with loosened hinges, an imp-shaped hole in the threshold rules, and a warning that the weather itself had an operator.

Outside, the storm continued without drifting. Its eye remained somewhere beyond the hedges.

Inside, nobody had decided whether a roof was safer than an ambush, whether the ping had found Archie or only his trail, or whether Remi would write a message to a home she could not address.

The night waited for an answer.

*The party had recovered the mirror, compromised the ward, received a threat from the Mazebounds, and opened a postal inquiry to a dimension without an address. This is what Disaster Inc. calls getting organized.*

aftermath:
## Immediate Position

The party holds the Mirror of True Reflection again, although the locating spell's response to the sleeping carrier rather than Archie remains unexplained. Tymnas's cottage is no longer secure: one window is shattered and covered by a closet door, the front hinges are damaged, and an imp demonstrated that an invited hostile already inside can authorize a vampire's entry. Randell escaped with severe radiant burns. Wario reports two dangers outside — a controlled storm and an arrest ambush — and recommends the storm's eye as the less predictable route.

## Custody

The Mirror is in party custody after Eager's theft. Wario supplied Remi a decoy crystal intended to be surrendered in place of the real one if she is captured. The transcript does not establish the real crystal's final holder clearly enough to amend its custody without qualification.

## Personal Carry-Forward

Remi has finally said aloud that she is not okay, does not know her home address, and does not know how to return to Kivotos. Wario offered message delivery if she can identify a destination. No message was completed before he returned to the catalog.
waluigiAssessment:
## Waluigi's Assessment

**The ping found custody, not necessarily Archie.** Markop's spell leading to the sleeping mirror carrier may mean the Mirror retains Archie's magical trail, may mean Archie touched it, or may mean the tracking premise is wrong. File the ambiguity; do not promote it into a rescue.

**Invitation wards are only as loyal as everyone already inside.** The imp in the closet converted Randell from excluded vampire to lawful guest with one sentence. Every warded safehouse containing prisoners, vermin, servants, summoned creatures, or hidden imps now has an invitation problem.

**Boundy knew Remi's name.** This is surveillance, shared memory, or tree-borne intelligence. The green apple is grotesque; the name is operationally important.

**Wario asked the correct question for the wrong reason.** He framed Remi's displacement as a threat to money flow, then made her answer whether she was okay. The motive does not cancel the result. The postal offer is real enough to pursue and dangerous enough to document.

**Final verdict:** the cottage remains a shelter only in the architectural sense. The party recovered an artifact and lost the certainty that doors, windows, names, weather, or invitations belong to them.

summary: The Mount Ebott Survey ends with an oath of silence, Wing Gaster's local-dimensional transport, a surface extraction, the handover of a survey machine that secretly logged conversations and battle readings, monitored outside communication privileges for the Gamma Agent, Mihawk's non-Legion debrief, an unauthorized Gamma interrogation over the Deadman's Stamp, Jamesly's intervention, Daniel's breach review, a High Command summons, and the final five recorded seconds before the logger is deliberately shut off.
description:
*"All recordings are now inactive."* — the last sentence on the Mount Ebott logger before High Command turned the archive off.

The final Mount Ebott log begins with a promise that the surface will not learn too much and ends with High Command making sure the archive cannot learn any more. That is the shape of the whole file: every institution in the room wants control over what may be known. Asgore and Toriel want monsterkind protected by silence. The Iron Legion wants the survey machine and all the data it secretly gathered. The Gamma Agent wants one hour a month to call home. Mihawk wants to leave with his dignity intact and without being made a prisoner for standing near a classified mission. Jamesly wants the Agent contained before talent becomes scandal. Daniel wants a discipline hearing until the Deadman's Stamp turns discipline into a leak investigation. High Command wants the final conversation off the public record.

The document therefore cannot be filed as a simple extraction. The extraction succeeds in the first half. The problem is what extraction *means* after the machine reaches Legion hands. A person can swear silence. A device cannot feel bound by an oath it was never told about. By the time the Gamma Agent understands that the survey machine has logged conversations, battles, energy levels, and monster technology, the Underground's secrecy has already been converted into a case file.

Waluigi files the final log as the moment the Mount Ebott survey stops being an expedition and becomes an argument about custody of knowledge. The party got out. The machine got out. The truth got out in a box. Then High Command closed the box on the archive itself.

The final log is also personal in ways its institutions try to sand flat. The Agent's request for outside communication is not merely a reward request; it is a person asking whether successful service buys the right to hear family again. Mihawk's quiet talk about an unnamed island is not merely biography; it is the sound of a man who has crossed a sealed world and still does not know where to stand next. Even the officer's fear matters. She is not only a source of information. She is a person learning that the manual she trusted was not the real manual. Waluigi files these things because an archive that records only protocols has already surrendered to the people who write protocols.

sections.name: The Oath That Made the Exit Legal
sections.overview:
Asgore did not treat the departure as a favor. He treated it as a risk with witnesses attached. His voice was steady because a king is expected to sound steady when saying dangerous things in a room that needs him steady. The Underground had endured for generations by remaining half rumor, half story, the kind of place the surface could dismiss as legend until curiosity became too expensive. If humans learned monsters were real, the old injuries could become fresh policy. Toriel made the same point with fewer ornaments and more finality: the oath was non-negotiable. Silence on what was seen. Silence on how they left. Silence not merely as etiquette but as survival.

The room waited for the answers. Sans swore first, quiet and firm, not because he had no doubts but because betrayal of monsterkind had no use to him after everything already lost. Mihawk answered in the way Mihawk answers many things: a single slow nod, arms crossed, loyalty reduced to the smallest motion that still counts. The Gamma Agent watched the others and the survey machine both. The oath entered the file as [[prop:prop_ebott_secrecy_oath|a contract made out loud]], but the machine sitting nearby was already becoming a second witness.

That tension is the entire seed of the final log. The Underground believed it was negotiating with people. It was. It was also negotiating in the presence of an object with broader memory than its operator understood. The Agent did not yet know that; ignorance is not malice. But ignorance does not delete a recording. Waluigi notes the oath as legally serious, morally serious, and structurally doomed the moment the wrong device crossed the threshold.

Then Asgore rose and the throne room moved from politics to mechanism. Toriel went to gather what was needed. The air changed. The farewell had become a procedure.
sections.waluigi_note: An oath before a machine is how serious people make a door. Waluigi prefers doors with hinges, but monarchs love ceremony. WAH.

sections.name: Gaster's Blaster Was a Door, Not a Gun
sections.overview:
The scientist entered like a man rolling in a holiday. Wing Gaster was squat, bright-eyed behind thick glasses, and wrapped in an apron that made the machine look less like an execution device and more like something a very excited baker had overbuilt. Blue lights pulsed along the frame. The apparatus hummed into the marble. Asgore watched with royal fatigue. Toriel returned solemnly, less interested in the scientist's pride than in the cost of success.

Gaster introduced himself as Royal Scientist and announced the CORE as his greatest creation. He was not simply preparing a transport; he was narrating the day he believed history would remember him for. The Agent whispered to Mihawk that the name sounded familiar. Mihawk considered the pirate Gaster from earlier in the expedition, measured the face, the manner, and the aura, and refused to overstate the resemblance. The scientist was cheerful, not cold. Names, however, are not common, and Mount Ebott had already taught the file that names can echo across impossible places without asking permission.

The platform lit. Mihawk stepped up first. Then the Gaster Blaster appeared beside Gaster and charged. In any sane room, a skull-shaped cannon materializing beside a scientist would end the conversation. Here, Gaster announced it as an invention: a stabilized dimensional projector for long-range transport. The blaster's beam struck the platform, swallowed Mihawk in light, and left the room with the terrible residue of dust-like shimmer.

The Agent checked the dust because under Mount Ebott dust has a history and a body count. Asgore said Mihawk was not dead. Toriel said he was simply elsewhere. Sans briefly called that elsewhere another world; the Agent corrected him. The surface was not another dimension. Gaster confirmed it: local-dimensional displacement within the same world's plane. This correction matters more than it first sounds. The Underground did not open a multiversal gate. It authorized a route to the surface. A gun-shaped door is still a door, and the oath applied to where it led.
sections.waluigi_note: The machine uses a skull cannon to do transportation. This is why scientists should be supervised by accountants and frightened gardeners.

sections.name: Koffin-K Arrived Too Late to Explain the Emergency
sections.overview:
The Agent stepped onto the platform after Mihawk. The room had already seen the procedure work once, which made it more frightening rather than less. The first transport proved the machine could take someone. It did not prove what else it could interrupt, attract, or leave behind. Gaster's hands moved quickly over the controls. The core brightened, throwing blue across Asgore's face. Toriel folded her hands. Sans received one look from the Agent, and whatever that look asked was never answered.

Gaster began the count. Three. Two. Then the door burst open hard enough to make the room forget the number after two. Koffin-K stood in the threshold with urgency stripped of theatre. He was not posing, boasting, or decorating his entrance with villain style. He shouted for them to wait. He said they could not send the Agent through yet. He said there was an emergency.

That is all the archive has. Gaster froze mid-countdown and asked what emergency. Asgore straightened. The room recognized the interruption as serious because Koffin-K had abandoned the performance by which everyone normally identified him. But the machine did not wait for the archive to receive a better sentence. The light took the Agent before the emergency could be named.

This is an unresolved lead, not a dramatic flourish. Koffin-K might have discovered a threat behind them, a consequence of Papyrus and Flowey, a failure in the transport, a political reversal, or something ridiculous delivered with perfect bad timing. The file cannot say. The investigation therefore keeps the warning as warning. Waluigi refuses to invent the missing content simply because the story wants a cleaner hinge. Sometimes the door opens, someone shouts, and history becomes light before the verb arrives.
sections.waluigi_note: A warning that arrives one syllable late is still evidence. It is also infuriating. File the interruption; do not invent the contents.

sections.name: The Machine Was Never Only Ecological
sections.overview:
The surface smelled like grass. That should have been the emotional center of the file: sky above, air moving naturally, birds in the distance, Mihawk already standing there and answering the Agent's question with a plain yes. They had done it. They had left the Underground without breaking the Barrier, without killing the King, without reducing the oath to a trick. For one breath, the mission could pretend to be complete.

Then the helicopter spotlight found them.

The Legion arrived cheerful and professional. The soldiers treated the extraction as a success because, from their side, it was. Target acquired. Data recovered. Assets alive. The Agent handed over the survey machine and the data packet. The receiving soldier secured them in a reinforced case and said the intelligence would change everything. That sentence is either praise or indictment depending on which side of the oath one is standing.

Only after the handoff did the machine's true scope become explicit. The Agent asked whether it had been meant to log battles, conversations, and other material. He had thought it was for ecological data. The soldier answered with a laugh: ecology, yes, but also conversations, battle readings, energy levels, monster tech scans. The receipt now filed as [[prop:prop_ebott_data_handover_receipt|the handover ledger]] confirms the mismatch. The Agent was not merely delivering what he believed he collected. He was delivering what the Legion's equipment had collected through him.

This does not make the Agent a liar. It makes him an instrument who was not told the instrument had another blade folded inside it. That is worse for the oath in a different way. Asgore and Toriel extracted a promise from people who could choose. The machine had already chosen nothing and remembered everything. Waluigi files this as the moment the survey mission's stated purpose collapses under its own hardware.
sections.waluigi_note: If your ecological scanner records conversations, it is not an ecological scanner. It is a clerk with a battery. WAH.

sections.name: The Embassy Sorted People Into Uses
sections.overview:
The embassy did not simply receive the expedition. It sorted it. The rooftop took the helicopter. The intake desk took the machine. The first briefing room took the Agent. The secondary chamber took Mihawk. Every hallway performed a small act of classification: asset, witness, non-Legion exposure, data carrier, command problem. The building's high-tech cleanliness is therefore not background decoration. It is the visual language of a place that wants all dirt converted into files before anyone can call it dirt.

The Agent enters with a machine and leaves the first room with a privilege. Mihawk enters with a sword and leaves with a surveillance problem attached. Neither outcome is random. The embassy knows how to reward a useful operator and how to make a polite cage for a useful witness. It does both without raising its voice. That is why the location gets its own record: not because the walls are interesting, but because the walls are part of the procedure.

Waluigi notes that the embassy's mirrored glass is almost too honest. A mirror lets one side watch while the other side sees only itself. That is exactly how the Legion uses debriefing here. The Agent thinks he is explaining the mission; the embassy is measuring the operator. Mihawk thinks he is answering whether he collected data; the embassy is deciding how much memory a free man is allowed to carry. The rooms are not passive. They are tools.
sections.waluigi_note: A building that separates witnesses before anyone asks is not a building. It is a questionnaire with elevators.

sections.name: The Flight That Refused Geography
sections.overview:
The High Command summons should have produced a long flight: borders, airspace clearances, fuel, time to think, time for the Agent to regret how much he had said to the embassy officer. The Agent even complains that the trip will cross a lot of borders for something that could have been handled by video call. The pilot answers with clearance. Then the world stops behaving like clearance is the hard part.

The helicopter reaches High Command too quickly. The Agent notices. He had expected days and gets arrival. He expected Mushroom Kingdom borders and gets a spire. The pilot does not explain. No guard stops him. The elevator rises at a speed that makes height feel like a rumor. By the time the chamber opens, the file has quietly changed genres again: this is no longer only a military chain of command. It is infrastructure that can cheat distance.

That matters because the Mount Ebott survey began as a geography problem. A mountain, a hole, a route down, a route out. The final movement is the opposite. High Command demonstrates that it can make distance collapse when it wants a Gamma Agent in a room. This turns the summons into more than orders. It is a display of reach. The Agent is not merely being called somewhere; he is being shown that 'somewhere' is negotiable for the people doing the calling.
sections.waluigi_note: When a helicopter trip skips the map, the map is either wrong or outranked. Waluigi dislikes both options.

sections.name: One Hour a Month, Monitored
sections.overview:
The embassy converted success into procedure. The building itself seemed designed to make the Agent's return feel less like rescue and more like intake: rooftop landing, sterile elevator, debriefing level, mirrored glass, officers too busy to stare for long but trained enough to know something valuable had arrived. The command officer praised the data dump as comprehensive. Analysts would study it for months. Years of field research had been saved by one machine and one under-briefed operator.

The Agent asked the only reward question that mattered to him: outside communication privileges. The officer hesitated, calculated, and granted them. One Legion-issued secure device. One hour per month. External calls allowed. Monitored by the duty officer and the authorizing command. Revocable on conduct. The [[prop:prop_gamma_comms_privilege|authorization]] is painfully precise because the Legion is most comfortable when kindness has a limit, a supervisor, and a clause.

The Agent accepted. Of course he accepted. The file notes his stated reason: he could finally contact his parents. The line should not be mocked. A monitored hour is still a voice crossing distance. It is also a leash made of minutes. The officer softened when family entered the conversation, and that softness was probably real. Institutions are cruelest when real people inside them can still feel sympathy but can only express it through forms.

This is why the communication device matters enough to file. It is not a shop item. It is not loot. It is a privilege granted because the machine delivered intelligence. The reward ties the Agent's private longing to the Legion's public appetite. Waluigi has seen worse bargains, but few that fit so neatly in one hand.
sections.waluigi_note: The Legion has discovered the smallest possible unit of mercy: sixty minutes, supervised.

sections.name: Mihawk's Debrief and the Problem of Being Nearby
sections.overview:
Mihawk's separation was inevitable. The soldiers had promised no detainment unless necessary, which is one of those sentences that sounds reassuring until one remembers who decides necessity. He was not Legion. He had seen the Underground, the transport, the machine, the extraction, and enough classified behavior to make a cautious institution itch. So he was placed in a secondary chamber, not a cell, and questioned by an officer whose politeness did not make the room less official.

The questions narrowed around role. How had he become involved? What was his connection to the data collector? Did he know what was being gathered? Did he assist in gathering ecological data, battle logs, conversations from monsters? Mihawk answered with the precision of a blade put back in its sheath. He did not collect the data. He was there to ensure safety. His role was protective, not analytical. The [[prop:prop_mihawk_debrief_summary|debrief summary]] accepts that statement and still marks him as exposed.

The lobby scene after the interview is quieter and in some ways more important. Mihawk and the Agent sit near the end of the mission and speak like men who understand that shared danger does not guarantee shared road. The Agent jokes that it truly was an under tale. Mihawk says they made it out with intel that changes things. He asks about the Agent's parents, then realizes the Agent had not told him that. It is a small misstep, but in a file about surveillance and inference, small missteps ring loudly.

Then Mihawk speaks of an unnamed island: isolated, fertile, peaceful, with lions and no formal claim. He had left young to become a pirate. He calls the sea freedom. The officer's later questions about his arrival at Mount Ebott meet only Mihawk's difficult answer: not planned, not coincidence, perhaps fate. To the Legion, this does not clear him. It makes him harder to categorize. A man without a named homeland who walked into a classified mountain and walked out beside a Gamma Agent is exactly the sort of person bureaucracy calls free while assigning someone to watch him.
sections.waluigi_note: The Legion believes a man can be free to walk and still worth watching. This is not contradiction to them. It is policy.

sections.name: The Deadman's Stamp Made the Room Smaller
sections.overview:
The embassy debrief became dangerous when the Agent stopped behaving like a rewarded subordinate and began testing the officer's clearance. The trigger was the mission's hidden casualty knowledge: two KIA, the dead authorizer, the orders that should not have been understood by the person in the room. The officer's professional tone cracked when the Agent implied knowledge she had not expected him to possess. She asked how he knew. That was the wrong question to ask a Gamma Agent who had begun measuring the ceiling.

The Agent pressed. If word got out about his true assignment, would that not be problematic? Was the officer even above the clearance level required to understand why Mihawk ended up at Mount Ebott? She summoned security. The Agent smiled, asked who was really in control, snapped his fingers, and used code Alpha Zeta 2, Protocol 6. The guards answered his command. The room's power diagram redrew itself in a second.

Then came the Real Manual. The Agent read from the hidden authority that ordinary officers had been trained to treat as myth: Article 9-4, Directive 6-Alpha, operation outside standard command, Article 13-7 and termination authority under the Deadman's Stamp. The officer collapsed under the realization that the book on the table was not the same law she had been taught. The [[prop:prop_real_gamma_manual_excerpt|extract]] is filed because it changes the genre of the scene. This is no longer a debrief about a mission. It is a demonstration that the Iron Legion contains a second chain of command with rules sharper than the visible one.

Jamesly's entrance prevents the scene from becoming only terror. He has enough authority to stop the Agent and enough familiarity to sound tired rather than surprised. He calls the Agent a loose cannon, an exceptional asset, and a complication. He names the actual violation: unauthorized interrogation of a civilian operative, execution protocols invoked without clearance. His intervention proves Gamma power has limits, but only limits enforced by people even deeper inside Gamma power.
sections.waluigi_note: When the secret manual is more important than the public manual, the public manual is a costume.

sections.name: The Officer Learned the Manual Was Not the Law
sections.overview:
The unnamed embassy officer begins the scene with ordinary authority. She has a desk, a pen, security within reach and a file she believes contains the relevant facts. That confidence does not survive contact with the Real Manual. The Agent's questions are not random intimidation; they are tests of what the officer knows, what she thinks she knows, and what her institution decided she did not deserve to know. The moment she recognizes the Deadman's Stamp, she changes from interviewer to evidence.

This is a cruel scene, and Waluigi will not pretend otherwise. The Agent pushes too hard. The guards are turned by code. The officer is frightened in a way that goes beyond professional discomfort. But the scene also reveals something the polite version would have hidden: the Legion trains some of its own people to believe the sharpest part of Gamma authority is a myth. When the Agent reads Article 13-7 aloud, the officer is not merely scared of the Agent. She is scared because the floor under her career opens and shows another floor beneath it, one she was never briefed on.

Jamesly calls the Agent reckless for good reason. He also arrives because the room has uncovered a real structural problem. The Legion's visible chain of command cannot supervise what it is not allowed to understand. That is why the officer matters even without a stable name. She is not a villain to defeat. She is the face of the institution discovering, too late, that it has been compartmentalized below the weapon it serves.
sections.waluigi_note: Fear is not proof. But when the trained officer panics at a clause she was told was myth, the panic becomes a filing.

sections.name: Protocol 4871 Made the Room Use Its Real Names
sections.overview:
Jamesly moves the problem into a darker room, and Daniel tries to make it a discipline hearing. The accusation is tidy: unauthorized interrogation, civilian operative, execution protocols, reckless behavior. The Agent does not deny the mess. He asks for procedure before defense: unsterilized names and a Gamma Observer under Protocol 4871.

This is one of the most important small moves in the log. Unsterilized names are not flavor. Sterilized names let institutions discuss people as categories until responsibility becomes fog. A Gamma Observer is not comfort. It is a witness the room cannot easily edit afterward. The Agent has just abused authority in one room and then uses authority correctly in the next to force the debrief to become auditable. Waluigi hates that both things are true, because clean moral sorting is easier to file and less accurate.

Daniel grants the request because protocol still binds him. That matters too. Gamma power is not pure chaos; it has rites, forms, countersignatures, observers, and vocabulary. The hidden state inside the state is still bureaucratic. It simply keeps a more dangerous set of forms. When the Agent names the Deadman's Stamp as a leak concern, Daniel's posture changes because the room now has the right names in it. The charge is no longer only that the Agent threatened someone. It is that someone outside the correct circle knew the threat existed.
sections.waluigi_note: A room that refuses real names is preparing to lie. A room forced to use them has at least been made to sweat honestly.

sections.name: The Breach High Command Would Not Let the Archive Hear
sections.overview:
High Command's chamber is not described for long because the chamber refuses to remain in the record. That refusal is itself a description. Three hooded figures, a circular room, the Agent walking quietly, a familiar voice thanking him for making the journey on short notice, and then the stated problem: an intelligence-network breach. A high-ranking Legion officer has been leaking classified information to an external party. Foreign operatives may be involved.

That is the kind of sentence the whole Mount Ebott survey has been walking toward without knowing it. The survey began as a descent into a hidden civilization, but the final threat is upward and inward: classified information leaving the Legion through someone with rank. Monsterkind's secrecy, the machine's over-recording, the Deadman's Stamp, Mihawk's exposure and the High Command summons are suddenly not separate loose threads. They are examples of the same disease: knowledge moving through channels that the visible authorities cannot fully control.

Then the Agent asks whether he should turn off his logger. High Command says yes. This is not merely operational caution. It is the first confirmed act by the people who claim to investigate the breach, and the act is to create another unlogged space. Waluigi will not claim that proves guilt. Waluigi will claim it proves method. High Command responds to a leak by making a room the archive cannot audit. Perhaps that is necessary. Perhaps it is incriminating. The only honest filing is to mark the moment the record goes dark and refuse to let darkness masquerade as nothing.
sections.waluigi_note: When the people investigating a leak begin by cutting the recorder, Waluigi writes down the scissors.

sections.name: The Summons and the Cutoff
sections.overview:
Jamesly moves the Agent into a higher room, and Daniel begins with discipline. The Agent asks for two procedural protections before the debrief: unsterilized names and a Gamma Observer under Protocol 4871. Daniel grants both, irritated but bound by the rules he still recognizes. That request matters. The Agent may be reckless, but he knows when to make the room use its real nouns. In a file where hidden manuals and false briefings are everywhere, unsterilized names are not courtesy. They are ammunition.

Daniel's accusation is simple: unauthorized interrogation, reckless conduct, protocol breach. The Agent answers with the Deadman's Stamp. The room changes again. If a civilian embassy operative knows that protocol, the issue is no longer only the Agent's conduct. It is leakage. Daniel asks how deep it goes. The Agent raises Mihawk as a factor: a pirate, a witness, someone who thinks the Agent inexperienced but has enough wit to be dangerous. Daniel orders surveillance. The investigation has now grown teeth on both sides: a possible internal leak and an external witness who cannot be allowed to drift unobserved.

A courier interrupts before the debrief can resolve. The [[prop:prop_high_command_summons|summons]] is direct: High Command wants the Agent in person. No video call. No substitute. No delay. The helicopter should have taken days and crossed borders; instead it arrives at the High Command spire almost immediately. The pilot knows the Agent's real name, James, and says they met during training. Geography folds. Procedure narrows.

At the top of the spire, three hooded figures wait. They announce an intelligence-network breach: a high-ranking Legion officer leaking classified information to an external party. The Agent asks whether to turn off his logger. They say yes. The last recorded seconds, preserved in [[prop:prop_final_logger_cutoff|the cutoff slip]], do not reveal the breach. They reveal the method by which the archive was denied the breach. That is enough. The final fact of Mount Ebott is not what High Command said next. It is that High Command knew there was a recorder and chose silence.
sections.waluigi_note: The final fact in the Mount Ebott survey is not what High Command said. It is that High Command knew where the recorder was and turned it off.
sections.imageCaption: The last visible act before the missing minutes: a hooded High Command official pressing the disabling device to the logger while the chamber watches.

aftermath:
## Immediate Position

The Mount Ebott survey team has left the Underground. That is the cleanest success in the file and the least complicated sentence anyone gets to keep. Mihawk and the Gamma Agent reached the surface alive. The transport did not require destroying the Barrier. Asgore and Toriel's egress condition was accepted. Wing Gaster's machine worked. Koffin-K's emergency did not stop the second transport.

Everything after that complicates the success.

## Custody

The recovered survey machine and data packet are in Iron Legion custody at the Old World Embassy. The handover receipt states that the device contains not only ecological readings but conversations, battle readings, energy levels and monster-technology scans. The Gamma Agent did not know the machine had that scope when he carried it through the Underground. This does not remove responsibility from the Legion. It relocates it from field behavior to equipment design and briefing.

The Gamma Agent retains a Legion-issued monitored communication device under a one-hour-per-month allowance. This is a real privilege and a real control mechanism. Both are filed.

Mihawk is not detained in the immediate record. He cooperated with debriefing and maintained that he served as protective support rather than data collector. Daniel's later surveillance order means he is not free in the way ordinary civilians use that word. He is free in the Legion sense: not in a cell, but in a file.

## Personnel and Standing

Jamesly has entered the active Gamma file as a senior handler able to interrupt the Agent. Daniel has entered as a command debrief authority who began with discipline and pivoted to breach review when the Deadman's Stamp became evidence of a leak. The unnamed embassy officer remains unpromoted to a character record because the log does not give a stable name and because her importance is procedural: she is the person whose knowledge reveals the leak risk.

## Open Threats

Koffin-K's emergency remains unknown. The Deadman's Stamp leak remains unresolved. Mihawk is a monitored witness. High Command's intelligence-network breach is established but not described because the logger was disabled at the threshold of the briefing. The missing minutes are not a gap in the archive's attention. They are an imposed silence.

## RNN and Follow-Up

The event has been added to the RNN pending list. No broadcast is cut from this single filing alone. The investigation file **The Oath, the Machine, and the Missing Minutes** now carries the evidence trail and should be the next place a reader goes if they want to argue with the silence.

## Emotional Carry-Forward

The Agent leaves this log with more authority than comfort. He has a phone privilege, but it is watched. He has High Command's attention, but not its trust. He has completed the survey, but the machine's hidden scope means success may have violated the spirit of the oath he just watched others swear. Mihawk leaves with less certainty than his composure suggests: no named homeland, no clear next port, and now a surveillance shadow because he stood close to the truth and did not flinch.

Waluigi's true discomfort is this: everyone in the final log is both helped and used. The Underground helps the visitors leave while using their silence. The Legion rewards the Agent while using his longing. The Agent frightens the officer while using her fear to test a leak. Jamesly saves the officer while using forgetfulness as cleanup. High Command calls the Agent while using darkness as a wall. This is not a clean victory. It is a successful extraction from one underground into another.
waluigiAssessment:
## Waluigi's Assessment

**The oath and the machine contradict each other.** Asgore and Toriel required silence because monsterkind's survival depends on remaining myth to the surface. That is understandable. Waluigi, who enjoys gossip, still understands why a hidden civilization does not want to become the subject of a bored empire's field study. But the survey machine had already made myth into data. The Agent's mouth could keep the oath. The machine's memory could not. This is why equipment design is diplomacy whether soldiers admit it or not.

**Wing Gaster's transport is cleaner than the institutions around it.** The Gaster Blaster looks like a weapon and behaves like a door. Disturbing? Yes. Efficient? Also yes. The science itself is almost honest compared to the politics that follow. It sends Mihawk and the Agent to the surface inside the same world's plane. It does not pretend to be a flower, a treaty, a phone call or a mercy. It does the one thing it says it will do. WAH! Waluigi did not expect to compliment the skull cannon.

**Koffin-K's interruption must not be thrown away.** A theatrical man arrived without theatrics and said there was an emergency. Then the transport took the Agent before the sentence could finish. That is not a joke. It is an uncollected debt. The next Ebott-adjacent filing should recover what Koffin-K meant or explicitly state that the warning was lost. An unexplained emergency is not flavor. It is a loaded shelf in a dark room.

**The communication privilege is both reward and leash.** One hour a month to call outside is meaningful. Waluigi will not sneer at a person wanting to contact family. But the conditions matter: monitored, revocable, justified by intelligence value. The Legion has turned longing into a compliance instrument. This is the sort of cruelty that smiles because it has technically helped.

**Mihawk is innocent of the wrong charge.** He did not gather data. He said so, and the record gives no reason to call that false. But the Legion is not only worried about guilt. It is worried about exposure. Mihawk saw the mission, the machine, the embassy, and enough of Gamma procedure to become dangerous by memory alone. His reward for honesty is surveillance consideration. Again: that is not contradiction in Legion logic. It is the point.

**The Real Manual is an empire inside the empire.** The Deadman's Stamp, Directive 6-Alpha, and Protocol 4871 reveal a hidden operating constitution. Public command still exists, but Gamma authority can step behind it, around it, and sometimes through it. The embassy officer's fear matters because she had been trained to treat part of the law as myth. When a state lies to its own officers about what its agents may do, the state is no longer keeping secrets from enemies. It is keeping secrets from its own hands.

**Final verdict:** the Mount Ebott Survey did not end when the team reached the surface. It ended when High Command turned off the logger. That is the moment the archive finally meets a wall built specifically for it. The file's last fact is therefore not the content of the breach briefing; the content is missing. The last fact is authorship of the silence. Someone with authority knew the logger existed, disabled it, and continued speaking. Waluigi cannot file what came next. Waluigi can file who made sure he could not.

summary: The morning after the wrong mountain, the taped-together charter is airborne with three passengers and a groggy pilot. Jory Dobbs opens a crate with a rusted dagger, gets a face full of orange flake, and then reads the stencils: PROPERTY OF WARIO WARE INC, on every barrel in the hold. Wario names it a corporate audit. The charter pilot trades a brass key and a crumpled VIP card for a silver canister's pulse in the fuel tank. The lights go green. Then the pilot says dimensional rift, three days to a refuel, and Heartstone, and Dobbs asks what is for dinner.

description: This is the second leaf of the One-T file. Part I ends with the charter coughing itself off Mount Ebot in hail. Part II begins in the air, with garlic, a wool cloak, and a calendar that has already moved on a day.

sections.name: I. Receding Peaks, and Garlic
sections.overview:
Dobbs sat by the cracked chin-bubble and watched Mount Ebot shrink. One T. The peak that had taken a night, a scalp, and a tail boom was already a grey knuckle in rain.

The cabin still smelled of onion sack and wet wool. The rotor beat through the floorboards. The charter pilot's hands were on the stick; they were not steady.

Wario let out a rattling sigh that made the seat complain. He found a squashed clove in his belt pouch and bit it. The crunch was the first cheerful sound since the cairn.

"Yeah," he said. "It's a real sight." The bite was gone from his voice. "That hill was a waste. Headache and a busted machine." He chuckled anyway. "We ain't done. When we find it, I'm the one with the biggest pile. Don't fall asleep on me."

He shut his eyes. His ears stayed open for the pilot.

Waluigi had his face on the cold glass. Snow-caps went to specks. His limbs did not fit the seat.

"Don't act like a hero, Jory." His voice cracked over the rotors. "If you hadn't been so *loud* with the punching, I wouldn't have had to lift the wiring." He turned on Wario. "And you. Stop being the boss. I kept this bucket in the air. Without me you'd still be down there letting that man nap until he froze."

He crossed his arms. "When we get the treasure I take a bigger cut. I'm tired of the work while he sits there looking *large*."

Dobbs pulled the tattered cloak tighter and asked how long the trip was.

"Who knows?" Waluigi snapped. "Shortcuts. The pilot is reading a map in a mirror. Fumes and good vibes. More than a few hours and I get cranky. Stay awake. I will not shake you at every bump."

From the front, Wario, eyes still shut: "Keep the bird moving. I'm hungry for more than garlic."
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi was in this room. He wants that stated, because Part I had to reconstruct the villa from other people's mouths. The glass was cold. The clove was real. The cut argument started before anyone had counted the crates.

sections.name: II. Anyone Coming to the Bin
sections.overview:
Dobbs stood up. The cloak snagged a rivet and came free. "Spare parts bin. Maybe there's something. Anyone coming."

Wario's eyes opened so fast his mustache jumped. "Now you're talking." The rest of the clove went in. He pointed a thick finger at the cramped alcove aft of the seats — plastic crates, a flicker bulb, the smell of old grease that had been in the machine since before the storm.

"I saw it when we loaded. Scrap means loot. Copper. Gears. Or parts so this junk stops dying. I'm going. If it's shiny I'm taking it." His boots hit the floorboards like unpaid invoices.

Waluigi unfolded with a pop of joints. "Obviously." He wiped grease off his chin with a tarnished handkerchief. "I'm not letting that lug hoard. Fairly divided. And if there are actual spare parts, maybe the rattling stops. My ears are ringing. Lead the way. Gold-plated gear is mine."

The alcove was as advertised: rusted gears, jagged plate, hydraulic pistons in weathered crates, one bulb doing its best. Oxidation sat on the tongue.

Dobbs put the rusted iron dagger to the first lid. The edge was notched. The crate was the same metal, only thicker.

The blade caught. Orange-red flake exploded. It coated the cloak, the pistons, Waluigi's handkerchief. The dagger stuck. The sound was a dull clink, not a shing.

Waluigi covered his ears. "A banshee with a chest cold! You are prying with dumpster iron. Move aside."

Dobbs moved aside.

Wario laughed until the bulb flickered. "Chocolate teapot." He did not use the dagger. He planted his feet, took the lid in both hands, and heaved. The hinges screamed. The lid hit the wall. *CRACK.*

"Give me something shiny."
sections.waluigi_note: *WAH!* The hire opened a Wario crate with a Wario dagger and was surprised when both objects agreed to be rust. Waluigi has opened jars with less theatre and more success.

sections.name: III. Pocket Change and Heavy Hitters
sections.imageCaption: First crate, lid off. Steel gear with an oily sheen at the bottom; Dobbs' brass coin already palmed. The bulb is the only witness that does not shout.
sections.overview:
Dobbs picked through the scatter while Wario mined. A jagged scrap of oxidized iron. A dull brass coin, emblem gone. He palmed both and looked at what the large man had decided was the venture.

Wario's hand closed on weight. He pulled up a heavy industrial gear — teeth still sharp, steel still holding an oily sheen under the grime — and a rectangular block of lead and brass that had come out of something expensive.

"Not junk. Collectors. Or we overhaul the lawnmower." He glanced at Dobbs' coin. "Pocket change. Wahaha."

Dobbs turned the coin once. "It was in the cargo hold. You packed it. How else does it get on the Wariocopter. Did we haul these without opening them."

Wario froze. The grin slipped. His eyes went crate, gear, Dobbs, wall.

"I— uh." Gravel in the throat. "A man of my stature does not dump things. System. Meticulous. Essential. Logistics. Weight. Aerodynamics. The shiny-factor. These were the best parts."

The laugh wheezed.

He leaned in. "Don't get philosophical. They're on the plane. Our loot. Packed or acquired — same result. Help me price them."

Dobbs looked at the unopened barrels. "All right. A system. You open. You give out what you think is useful."

Wario's shoulders dropped, then inflated. "Fine. I can do organized. Master of Goods. You watch for surprises. I lift. I think. Streamlined." He grabbed the next crate. "Prepare for distribution."
sections.waluigi_note: Dobbs asked the only question that matters on a charter you loaded yourself: who put the treasure in the treasure hunt. Wario answered with aerodynamics. Waluigi files that as a confession with extra syllables.

sections.name: IV. The Wario-System
sections.overview:
The second crate was wood and rusted bands. Wario shoved it to the centre. Dust. He came up with a soot-covered industrial wrench, notched head, built for work that leaves marks.

"You. Swinging. Unscrewing. Tool of the trade." He tossed it. Dobbs caught the weight against his chest.

Wario's face lit on a small leather pouch that sat heavy, and a coil of high-tensile wire. Both went into his own belt.

"Strategic supplies. Emergency weight management."

Waluigi had been on the bulkhead the whole time. He pushed off. His shadow cut the scrap into long pieces.

"Bravo. A system. Charity for the delusional. He gives you the lifting and keeps the steal-later. You are his mule. Do not let the voice fool you."

He ignored the wrench. He pointed into a corner Wario had not emptied: a small silver canister, pressurized, light enough for a pocket.

"If you want to be useful, take that. Coolant. Lubricant. Worth something when the engine screams. Wario — drop that gear on my toes again and your next meal is unseasoned crackers."

There was a [[prop:prop_ebot_p2_calendar|calendar in the junk]]. Dobbs read it before he moved.

18 Aethel, 1032 BF.

The day after the plank.

He went for the canister.

Wario threw his head back until the mustache touched his chest. "Another expert. Fine. Take the tin. Probably perfume so the pilot doesn't smell like a locker room. Don't spill it on the boots. High-quality leather."

He went back into the crate with both arms.

Waluigi's eyebrows went up, then settled into smug. "A modicum of sense. Don't get comfortable. You're still a liability in a cloak. Wario — stop pulling like a caveman."
sections.waluigi_note: Waluigi pointed at the only object in the crate that could still do a job. Wario kept the pouch. The calendar is why this leaf is dated the 18th and not 'the next morning' — Dobbs read the paper, which is more than Wario did with the stencils.

sections.name: V. PROPERTY OF WARIO WARE INC
sections.imageCaption: Brass fitting and frayed data cable, stencil intact. PROPERTY OF WARIO WARE INC. The joke is that the room agrees.
sections.overview:
Waluigi put Dobbs on small metal. "Jewelry of the machine world. Brass. Copper. If it aches the back, Wario can have it. Data cables under that piston — light, stashable. Lazy loaders dump waste on top."

Dobbs opened the next box. Tangled multi-coloured cable, frayed, intact. A brass fitting. He turned the fitting to the bulb.

The stencil was still readable.

[[prop:prop_ebot_warioware_stencil|PROPERTY OF WARIO WARE INC.]]

Wario's neck muscles stood out. He lunged and took the cable in a vice.

"That's-a my property. Secure bin. Not for rummaging. Handling fee." He shook it at Waluigi. "Don't laugh. I know what you're pricing."

Dobbs did not argue the cable. He looked at the rest of the alcove.

Every crate. Every barrel. The same stencil, or a cousin of it. WarioWare. Wario Ware Inc. Property of.

Wario's face went red, then white. He clutched his head. The charter shuddered under his pacing.

"Everything? Inventory like confetti. Guards asleep. Pilot sold it. The kingdom stole it." He stopped. The eyes narrowed. "Wait. If it's all mine we aren't scavenging. We're reclaiming. Corporate audit. Aggressive. Recovery team. Start hauling."

He slung a crate of gears over one shoulder as if the argument had been about weight all along.

Waluigi cackled. "A thief with a better excuse. Tell the authorities 'reclaiming' and they still call it a heist. However." He traced a barrel rim. "The logistics are favourable. We aren't stealing from the kingdom. We are gathering assets. Organize them, you idiot. Electronics together. Heavy scrap back."

Dobbs was already turning toward the seats. "We're in the air. No one is going to check. You or Wario brought it. Pointless. How far to Ebott." Two T. The right mountain. "I'm going to the luxury seating."
sections.waluigi_note: *WAH!* He labelled his own hold, forgot he had labelled it, and then billed the discovery as an audit. Waluigi has seen better bookkeeping in a sock.

sections.name: VI. The Pilot's Personal Request
sections.overview:
Wario's crate tilted. He set it down with a thud that made the floorboards groan. Relief came out of him like a puncture.

"You're-a right. Hidden route. If no one sees it, it never happened. Perfect crime. Or perfect audit." He stayed with the barrels. "Go sit. I'll make sure no one snoops. Don't sleep. Real lifting later. Distance — I don't know the miles. Profit when we land."

The luxury seating was the part of the charter that still pretended to be a company: velvet that had been crimson once, a low table, the smell of old tobacco trying to cover hydraulic fluid.

The cabin door creaked. The charter pilot leaned on the frame. Grease overalls. He did not look at the crates. He looked at Dobbs.

"Hey, kid. Official, I know. Fuel sensors are acting up. Kingdom tech. I need a steady source for the navigation lights over the mountains. I saw the canister."

Waluigi stood as if he had been invited onto a stage. "Mechanical tantrum. Tragic. I can be a hero for smooth sailing. Official record. I don't work free. Extra attention to cargo safety."

Dobbs cut across him. "I can help. In exchange for money."

The pilot's mouth twitched. One yellow eye — the crash had left him a colour. "Money speaks. I can't give you a treasury. I can leave blind spots on the manifests. Canister to the main terminal. Pressurized. Sync the valve with the auxiliary output. Wrong, and navigation is the least of it."

He put a tarnished brass key on Dobbs' palm. "Maintenance locker. Bypass kit. If Wario asks why the lights stopped flickering, tell him you're optimizing. He'll believe anything that keeps loot safe."

The key was still warm from the overalls pocket.
sections.waluigi_note: The man who flew them into a cave now sells 'blind spots' for a tin of coolant. Waluigi wanted the consultation fee. Dobbs asked for money out loud, which is the only language that has ever worked on this aircraft.

sections.name: VII. Brains, Brawn, Delicate
sections.overview:
Dobbs spun the key. "Waluigi. Split it and come, or stay."

Waluigi was on his feet before the word *split* had finished. "Favourite language. We go. I watch the distribution. Technical consultant. You negotiate."

"Wario is coming too," Dobbs said. "Less money for me. Maintenance room. Cores."

The engine pit was a trench of ozone and grease. Sodium lamps. Oil in rainbow slicks. Hydraulic pistons in the walls. Wario's boots rang on the grating.

"This is work. Dump full of opportunity. Squeeze the pilot. Lead."

Dobbs pointed Waluigi at the locker. The key ground, then turned. Inside: rusted tools, rags, a heavy metal case that hit a crate with a thump.

"Magic kit," Waluigi said. "Wires. Wrenches. I tinker. You lift. Don't let his paws near the wiring."

Dobbs looked at the three of them. "I get it. I'm the brains. Wario is the brawn. You're the… delicate one." He found a folded note in the kit, read it to himself, and tossed it. The goods were a grease-stained rag and a small copper bundle.

Wario's laugh shook the pipes. Gold tooth. "Brains, brawn, delicate. Nice ring. Premium brawn. Move."

The pilot had followed them down. He leaned on a pillar with his arms folded. Cold. "Let's not get ahead of ourselves with the titles."

Dobbs hissed. "If you're just watching, what's the point of us helping you." He took the rag and the wire. He took the key back off the locker door and pocketed it.

Wario went crimson, then delighted. "Feisty. Tell me where to put my weight." He took the copper bundle. The strands groaned.

"Nearly twenty-three," Dobbs said. "Don't get excited." He put the rag to the housing.

The grease went on too thick, or in the wrong place. The contact smeared. The rag tore.

The pilot's yellow eye tracked the hands. "Smart to try. Don't jam it. Heat will seize the gears over the next ridge. Even. Clean contacts, not wet. I am not flying a gorge in the dark."
sections.waluigi_note: Dobbs named the jobs correctly and then failed a rag, which is the most honest sequence in the leaf. The note in the kit was not filed. If it mattered, someone would have kept it. They kept the key.

sections.name: VIII. Fuel Tank A1
sections.imageCaption: Fuel Tank A1: rusted reservoir, iridescent oil, sodium lamps. The silver canister is at the auxiliary valve. The screen is not yet green.
sections.overview:
Dobbs packed the kit. "Fuel tank. This should be everything."

The walk from the industrial landing block to Wario's private dock was a corridor that tasted of burnt oil. Ten minutes. Wario talked the whole way about schedules.

Fuel Tank A1 was a chamber with a rusted steel reservoir slick as a soap bubble and fumes you could chew. Piping. Pressure valves. Sodium lamps making long shadows.

Wario whistled. "A vein of loot. Grime — which valve pays without bringing the ceiling down."

He had started using a name for the pilot. The archive does not. The man in the overalls did not correct him.

"Those aren't handles. Pressure-regulated. Wrong crank, and you wear industrial accident. I check flow first. You." He meant Dobbs. "Brains today. Watch the gauge on that canister while I hook the main line. Needle in the red — you say so before the pipes scream. You" — Wario — "stay back unless you want to be dragged out of a ceiling."

Dobbs stepped to Waluigi and dropped his voice. "What's the point of him paying us if he's helping anyway. Shouldn't the pilot be piloting." Then, to himself, loud enough: "Sync the pressure valve with the auxiliary output. Main terminal." He looked at the screen on the tank.

Waluigi's whisper was a rasp. "He isn't doing a favour. He's a tool Wario is squeezing. He pays so he still feels in charge. He flies just enough that we don't hit a crevasse. Focus on the valve."

The pilot heard the vibration of it. He came off the doorframe. "A lot of noise for the brains. I don't have time for philosophy. Kingdom grid is garbage. Sync it. I want those lights steady."
sections.waluigi_note: Dobbs asked why a paid man was doing the work he had paid for. Waluigi's answer was unkind and accurate. The archive leaves the pilot unnamed; Wario's nickname is not a character page.

sections.name: IX. All Clear
sections.overview:
Dobbs set the canister at the auxiliary fitting as if it might bite. Wario loomed until the panel was all mustache.

"Break it and I dock your pay."

"You're docking my non-existent pay," Dobbs said, and shoved.

A spark. A whine. The screen flickered hard. Wario's knees remembered the cave.

"Hardware! Green before the wind."

Waluigi laughed from a rib of the fuselage. "Let him scream. Left. You're fighting the pressure. Brains, remember."

Dobbs moved a fraction left and read the screen out loud: bar graph, line graph, a red light, a yellow light, a green light, all three lit at once.

He hesitated. "Looks fine. Let's talk payment."

The pilot's jaw tightened. "Fine is not a number. I want the delta on the variance. Hairpin on the line mid-ascent and *fine* is the last word on the mountainside. Payment is between the owner and the muscle. You stick to dials."

Wario and the pilot stepped back. Dobbs spun the calibrations. "Fields within acceptable bounds, wouldn't you say, Purple Stache. Flux is — no. Normal operational range. Sustaining."

"*Wah!* Nicknames." Wario's pat nearly folded him. "If it's acceptable it's Wario-approved. Heartstone. Stay green. Yellow is your repair bill."

Waluigi: "He sees green as go. Watch the variance. I am watching your value."

The pilot slammed a wrench on a pipe. "Enough. Needles in the red, the tank vents. Gauge. Steady."

Dobbs turned dial A1 to B2, C9 to I2, flux flow to twenty percent, industrial mixer on. The lights went green, one after another. A ding.

All clear.

He sighed.

Waluigi squinted at twenty percent as if it were an insult. "A whisper. Better than the next dimension. Not the hero. Grunt work."

Wario's hand on the shoulder was a shove. "Oversized head paying off. Commission when we find the Heartstone. Don't tell Waluigi. Get the bird moving."
sections.waluigi_note: *WAH!* He called me Purple Stache to my brother's face and then made the tank say All Clear at a whisper. Waluigi will allow the nickname. He will not allow twenty percent to be called heroism.

sections.name: X. Dinner, and the Rift
sections.overview:
They took the long talk back to the cockpit: oil-slick analog, flickering CRTs, wiring in the dash like veins, red warning lights still pulsing out of habit.

Dobbs found the crumpled [[prop:prop_ebot_vip_clearance|VIP clearance]] in his pocket. The pilot pretended not to see it. Dobbs bit the hardened ration. It tasted like the box it came in.

Wario wrinkled his nose. "Sawdust. That paper doesn't make you boss. If it gets us past guards, fine. Security chumps get a corporate statement. I throw them."

The pilot hunched over the nav console. Yellow eye on the altimeter. "Mouth shut. Eyes forward. Chew quietly. Wario — your voice is on the sensors. Hot zone."

Dobbs looked at the map. "Refueling zone. Three days. What's for dinner."

The pilot's laugh had no humour. The housing rang under his hand. "Dinner. You think this is a tour. You think I plate a meal over a dimensional rift. You eat what Wario scavenges. We're on fumes into a dead zone. Heartstone with a side of steak if you must pray. I know the map. Sit down."

Waluigi groaned theatrically. "A grumpy pilot who thinks he's why we aren't pancakes, and a human worried about his tummy. His grump is how he stays in charge. I want treasure, not three days of biscuits."

Dobbs stopped chewing. "Hold up. Dimensional rift. I asked for dinner because I am hungry." The second bite of ration failed him — dry, stuck, eyes watering. "We can't gloss that. Where are we stopping. Game plan. I never heard this."

Waluigi scoffed. "Not a scenic tour. Not our backyard, you thick-headed human. The rift is why the scenery is a fever dream and why this mountain shouldn't be on our maps. Summit. Wario's shiny rock — Heartstone. I keep us from glaciers and cave weirdos while he counts coins that aren't there. Don't choke. He'll treat you as cargo."

"First," Dobbs said, "you say human like you're not one. Second, I'm going to see if there's food in storage. You can handle your little dimensional rifts alone."

Waluigi's face did the offended disbelief. "Excuse me. Masterpiece of biology. Proportions. Not a peasant from your side of the rift. Handle it alone — I'm why this junk isn't a lawn ornament. Go play scavenger hunt. Don't cry when it's cardboard and grease. *Waaaah.*"

Dobbs went aft toward storage. The lights stayed green. The map still said three days. The rift did not get a second sentence from the man flying.
sections.waluigi_note: The hire asked the question the villa briefing skipped: what world is this. Waluigi answered with Heartstone and proportions. The file ends with Dobbs hunting dinner, which is the correct priority when the last honest meal was a wrapped loaf on a crashing floor.

outcome: Airborne. Navigation lights holding on a twenty-percent pulse from a silver canister that was already in Wario's own hold. Wario in possession of a steel gear, a lead-brass block, a heavy pouch, wire, and a legal theory called audit. Dobbs in possession of a wrench, scrap, a dull coin, a brass key, a VIP card, and the knowledge that every stencil in the alcove already said WarioWare. Waluigi in possession of the argument. The charter pilot in possession of the stick and a sentence he had not used on the 17th: dimensional rift. Destination still Mount Ebott, two T. Heartstone unnamed on any chart in the file. Three days to a refuel. Dinner not served.
notableFeatures: Calendar in the junk: 18 Aethel, 1032 BF
Rusted dagger fails; rust shower; Wario opens the crate by hand
Every crate stencilled PROPERTY OF WARIO WARE INC
Wario-System: wrench to Dobbs, pouch and wire to Wario
Silver canister overlooked, taken on Waluigi's point
Brass key and VIP clearance traded for a nav pulse
All Clear at twenty percent flux
Pilot names a dimensional rift and a Heartstone; Dobbs asks for dinner
aftermath: Standing: the party remains three plus one unnamed charter pilot, still unpaid, still pointed at the mountain with two T. Materiel: WarioWare inventory 'reclaimed' in place; canister committed to the auxiliary valve; VIP card in Dobbs' pocket; key in Dobbs' pocket. Exposure: the pilot now speaks of a rift and a Heartstone that were not on the 17th's briefing table. The wrong mountain is behind them. The right one is not yet under the skids.
waluigiAssessment: 1. Wario packed his own company property, forgot, looted it, and renamed the forgetting an audit. The stencil is the finding. 2. Dobbs is the only person on the aircraft who reads labels, calendars, and maps in that order. 3. The silver canister was the only object in the hold still able to do work; Waluigi pointed; Dobbs took it; the lights went green. That is the whole technical plot. 4. The charter pilot is not a new character. He is the same concussed man from Part I, now selling blind spots. Wario's nickname for him is not canon. 5. 'Dimensional rift' and 'Heartstone' enter the file as speech, not as surveyed fact. Recommendation: keep the One-T file open until someone puts a Heartstone on a table that is not Wario's imagination.
