outcome: The Overgrown Library was retaken - the first room in the manor anybody chose to defend for its own sake rather than as a route somewhere else. The shambling mound that was eating the collection was killed by a goblin staff, a warhammer and a magic missile, and was already most of the way dead when the party arrived. A second plant creature, posing as the lady of the manor behind a bathroom door, was destroyed with a single spark of fire. The mushroom room was confirmed to have an effect its own guards deny and its mushrooms do not carry. A violet fungus was recovered from an upstairs toilet, untranslated. aftermath:
The library is held and nobody is holding it. The party retook a room, looted a corpse for a pointy stick, and walked out of it toward the planning room without leaving a guard, which means the reclamation is currently a sentence in this filing rather than a fact on the ground.

Three threads leave this session open. The first is Red: she has a working counter-strategy, an operating supply line, and a key to the main room, and nobody has yet asked her the obvious question, which is whether the heir knows what she is cooking. The second is the mushroom room, where the fungus tests clean and the men do not, and where a guard misjudged how long he had. The third is Toad Lee, who has now lost time in combat three times, and whose "I still want to be safe with Hjumpik" was delivered with nothing at all behind the eyes.

The violet fungus is uncatalogued and untranslated. The circular passage has not been re-entered. And the standing order - upstairs, the main room, the heir, the plan built on a tactical map over a whole night - has now been abandoned for a full session and replaced with nothing.
waluigiAssessment:
**1. The victory was not one, and I used that against him and then against myself.** A shambling mound already fought by the fey residents, then stabbed by a goblin staff, then hit by a warhammer, then detonated by me, is not a trophy. It is a queue. I said so, and I was right. Then Hjumpik said *we can't fight every battle* - the dwarf, the one who hjumps on things, counselling restraint at me - and I answered *if they're that weak we should take them on*, which is the exact reasoning that gets parties killed, and which I had disproved myself ninety seconds earlier. He put a hand out. I opened the door anyway. The thing behind it was not weak at all. The archive records that the Auditor-General won the argument on the facts and lost it on the only question that mattered.

**2. Hjumpik abandoned a night's planning for a room full of books and it was the right call.** *Not my library.* Three words, no deliberation. The archive has spent four sessions watching this house treat every room as a corridor to somewhere better, and the dwarf is the first person in it to defend a place because it was worth defending. It cost us the upstairs plan. File it as a loss in the ledger and a gain in every other column.

**3. The cook is winning and nobody upstairs knows.** Red has what the war room does not: a delivery system the enemy already trusts. The heir has pins. She has a poison the overgrowth eats voluntarily, at scale, on a schedule. If this manor survives, it will not be because of the sixth and seventh divisions. It will be because somebody kept making dinner. RECOMMENDATION: get her a second cook and get out of her way.

**4. Toad Lee, third instance.** The missing hours. *I swung out of instinct.* And now a question asked twice over a body he was looting. Three is not a pattern the archive can keep calling a coincidence, and Morel's warning about anchors was specific. Somebody needs to sit down with him while he is definitely himself, and somebody needs to decide what we do if that stops being a thing we can schedule.

**5. The passage went in a circle and the house meant it.** Three knocks the dwarf was taught and could not reproduce. Others already waiting in the dark. Everyone deposited back on their own doorstep. This house has a functioning hidden infrastructure that opens for its own people and returns strangers to where they started, and we have been walking around inside it for weeks congratulating ourselves on our stealth.

**6. On the sentence.** I said I could not afford not to care anymore. I said it in a corridor, over a roar, to a dwarf who had just asked me since when - and he asked it *because* I had spent the whole night telling him caution was killing us and had then opened a door to prove it. The question was not rhetorical. It was a man looking at somebody who had just behaved completely out of character and asking, reasonably, what had changed. What changed was volume eleven, and a finger under the line. RECOMMENDATION: none. There is no recommendation. WAH.

summary: Waluigi's morning filing reviewed an abridged newspaper clipping that ended with a successful portal home. The full account recovered the same evening contradicts that ending: the portal failed, Luigi vanished during a strange tape, a corrupted Mario stepped out of the television, and Wario's Apparition ran a song-laden game show before a Wario Inc. tablet's flashlight ended it. description:
Waluigi stopped at the name: [[prop:prop_promo_mario_newspaper_clipping|PROMO MARIO]]. The available newspaper account supplies no publisher, byline or issue date. It supplies churros, souvenir shirts and a very helpful corporation.

## What the paper says

Lord Darian Marsh of the Dark Shores and Alistair of the Marshkeepers reportedly fell onto the set of the Nintendo Mania pilot. Their host introduced himself as Mario, taught them a video game and took them around Hollywood. Alistair collected souvenirs; Darian wanted proof of the journey, then a way home to his province.

The turn came with a Wario Inc. tablet. Darian displayed [Waluigi's account of the missing Mario](#/article/mario). The host read about Peach's assassination and the [Star Fountain reunion](#/article/star_fountain_reunion), dropped his phone and wept. Asked whether he was that Mario, he offered a name—not a remembered journey. His Luigi arrived with pizza; he said Peach was alive in the studio.

The report ends with Miyamoto arranging help and Dr. Takeda opening a sixty-second portal. Darian and Alistair stepped through with Nintendo charms. **Mario stayed behind.** The paper does not describe our missing hero coming home.

## What Waluigi can actually file

*WAH! I recognize the tablet passage. It is MY writing. A man crying after reading my article is not a second witness to the events in it. I would like Mario found, even if it means another unbearable celebration without me. This is not enough.*

Alistair also places Mario's disappearance in 955 BF. That is the year of [Peach's assassination](#/article/princess_peach); the archive places the fountain meeting in 1039 BF. A matching cap and brother do not settle that contradiction. The claimed souvenirs and photographs have not been authenticated here, and Peach never appears before the visitors in the account. Like the [charred note](#/article/charred_note_at_waluigis_door), this is another story to test, not permission to replace the old file.

waluigiAssessment:
**The mistake, filed honestly.** This is the assessment I should have written this morning, and I could not write it then because I did not know the morning was incomplete. I filed a reading of a reading. The newspaper was itself abridged — it ended at the first happy beat — and I treated a headline as a source. That is the whole failure, and I will not dilute it by blaming the paper alone.

1. **I never asked for the rest of the article.** A clipping with a clean ending is a bid, not a report. The full account shows the paper cut the portal failure, the tape, the missing brother, the corrupted Mario and an entire Wario song cycle. One question — *what happened after the farewell?* — was the whole file.
2. **The date error was a clue, not the error.** I filed 955 BF as a flaw in an unverified clipping. The full account treats 955 BF as the disappearance year, and it does so insistently. That is a claim, not a typo. Somebody in that world has been told the assassination and the disappearance were the same event — which is exactly what the charred note wants the archive to believe, and exactly what the archive does not believe about the 1039 BF fountain.
3. **The ending was the tell.** A corporate rescue with a sixty-second portal, crying staff and a generous goodbye is a good ending. It is so good that I stopped checking whether the machine worked. The portal did not open. I filed the goodbye and left the machine out of the record.
4. **What the fuller account does not fix.** Darian and Alistair remain one source. The studio Mario is still not proven to be our Mario. The Doughnut World reading is Darian's theory, not a documented plane. The figure that came out of the television is not filed as a Mario at all — it is filed as something that wears the name.
5. **What I actually learned.** I am not the only person who can be misled by my own archive. A man in another layer of the world read my article and cried at it. I will spend some time deciding whether that makes my article good.

**Recommendation:** find Luigi; obtain the original tape and the security footage; interview Darian and Alistair separately; and do not go to the exit, because every exit in that building is a trap.

revisions.body:
> **Amendment, 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — evening.** Revision 1 stays above, word for word, because it is what I filed when I had half a page. This is Revision 2: the full account [[prop:prop_promo_mario_full_account|that reached the archive this evening]]. It is longer, it contradicts the newspaper's ending, and it contains a Wario song cycle that the clipping had quietly removed. I am filing it tonight — on the day I found out how much I had missed, not on the day I stopped being embarrassed about it. WAH.

## Part One: Two People Fall Out of the Sky

Mario was reading a book when the lights above the sound stage flickered twice, and two figures dropped out of nowhere, hit the floor of the **Nintendo Mania** pilot set, and lay still long enough for a stagehand to scream.

He looked up. He closed the book. He crossed the floor with the careful cheer of a man who has decided the alternative is a lawsuit.

"Oh! Uh—Hey paisanos! I'm Mario!" He spread his arms wide. "But you probably knew that already."

The taller of the two strangers — fine dark clothes, a noble's collar, dust still settling in his hair — was staring at the cameras. The shorter one, a steward, had his hand on a weapon that did not exist in this building.

Mario studied the pair. Then he glanced at the camera, squared his shoulders, and did what he always did when the lights were hot and the answer was missing. He performed.

"Now, you may be wondering—" he said, and stopped. "Two people fall in from the sky, unknown to him. Sorry, who are these guys again?" He turned to the camera, waited, nodded as though the answer had arrived. "Oh, right. So anyways—you and your friend here arrived at a very *curtail* moment. **Promo Mario!** "

The director's voice came off the floor speakers, tired: "Mario, that's not a segment."

"Shhh. It's a *moment.*"

*WAH! He has been the most famous man in his world for so long that he cannot tell the difference between a rescue and a television bit. I used to find this charming. I am rereading it at midnight and I find it terrifying.*

## Part Two: A Name From the Dark Shores

The host's composure lasted one more beat. He clapped his hands, spun in place, and knocked his own chair over with a *clatter*.

"Mamma mia! The suspense is killing me—like when you run out of 1-Up mushrooms in the castle level!" He grabbed both strangers by the shoulders. "Tell-a me, tell-a me—are you from another dimension? Time travelers? Maybe secret Nintendo testers sent to spy on my show?"

Neither answered. Mario spun and began pacing, counting on his fingers.

"I mean, look at this setup—brand new pilot episode filming today! First ever footage of Luigi *playable*, and that cool cutscene where Peach gets kidnapped by Bowser!"

The director yelled, "Action!" Mario snapped into host mode, arms out, teeth bright.

"So what do ya say, folks? Ready to see some gaming history?"

The stranger in the dark clothes did not say anything about gaming history. He said: "I am sorry. I don't really understand."

Mario's grin folded. "Oh no, oh no! Did I go too fast again? Like when you play Super Mario 64 and forget to press Z for camera control?" He lowered the stranger into a director's chair, grabbed a bottle of water from the craft table, and crouched. "Okay, okay. Let me explain slow-like. You fell from *sky-boom*!" He made an explosion shape with both hands. "You landed in the middle of my show's filming day! Nintendo Mania! Pilot episode!"

Technicians moved past with light meters. Somewhere on the far side of the set a microphone *screeched*.

"But don't worry, amigo." He patted the stranger's shoulder. "We'll figure this out together."

The stranger looked at his steward. The steward looked back. Neither looked convinced.

## Part Three: Darian Marsh, and the Man Who Bows

The stranger rose, brushed the dust from his sleeve, and offered a bow that belonged in a throne room rather than a sound stage.

"Darian Marsh of the Dark Shores, at your service. And this here is my steward." He gestured. "Introduce yourself for me, young man."

Mario's eyes went wide — comically, exactly the size they went when he collected one hundred coins in *Mario Bros.* "Darian Marsh?! The Dark Shores?!" He snapped to rigid attention, hands clasped.

The steward stepped forward, hesitated, and bowed the way a soldier bows when he intends to be remembered. "I am Alistair of the Marshkeepers, sworn protector of Lord Darian."

A hush dropped over the set. A technician stopped mid-cable. The director turned slowly from his monitor.

Mario's jaw came open. He removed his red cap and held it over his heart.

"...Mamma mia..." He said it like a prayer and a warning at once. "This—this is bigger than finding all twelve Power Stars..."

*WAH! Twelve. He said twelve. There are twelve Power Stars in that game and I know this because I have had to hear about that game for ten consecutive evenings. The point is: a man with a title made the host treat him like royalty, and nobody on that set asked why a noble of the Dark Shores had a steward with a sword and no invitation. Nobody. Including me, apparently, for an entire morning.*

## Part Four: The City Through the Window

Darian looked past the host, past the lights, past the green screens, and asked the question that would have saved everyone an evening if it had come earlier.

"Well. We're in the Midlands. Which part is this?"

Mario did a double-take. "Midlands? Uh—" He scratched his head. The director facepalmed behind him. "Wellll... no, no! This is Hollywood!" He waved at the sound stages. "You're like... way off course! Like when you warp to Bowser's Castle instead of Peach's!"

Then he snapped his fingers. "But hey—maybe that explains how you fell from sky-boom!"

The tall windows ran the length of the far wall, and Mario threw them open. Los Angeles came in with the wind — skyscrapers stacked against a sunset, palm trees black against the light, cars moving like spilled beads, mountains in the distance, and one silver plane dragging a white thread across the sky.

Alistair pressed his palms to the glass and went very quiet.

"This place is huge," Darian said. It was the first thing he had said without a title in it.

"Big, huh?" Mario grinned. "Wait till you see Times Square! The whole city is bigger than your whole kingdom, probably!"

Alistair's voice was barely audible. "It's so many people and buildings..."

Mario bounced on his heels. "Hey! Wanna go outside? We could show you around properly!"

The director began, "Mario, the schedule—"

Mario ignored the schedule. Mario always ignored the schedule. This is the detail that I kept circling all evening, because ignoring the schedule is exactly what a host does when he has decided the day is content.

## Part Five: A Churro and a Street Full of Machines

The Hollywood sidewalk was a sensory assault: billboards flashing, neon signs stacked on neon signs, traffic humming, an ice cream truck playing a tune out of tune, and a street vendor selling hot dogs whose smell crossed the whole block.

Mario walked ahead, one arm out like a tour guide who has never once been paid for a tour. "That's Grauman's Chinese Theater! See the celebrity handprints?"

Behind him, Alistair leaned close to Darian. "Milord... it's like the whole kingdom has been squeezed into these moving metal boxes. But there are thousands of them."

"Don't worry," Darian said quietly. "They're all going somewhere. That's what we're trying to do, remember?"

Mario had already stopped at a pink food truck. He came back holding two churros dusted in cinnamon sugar, one of which he pressed into Darian's hands. "Here! Best snack ever!"

Darian took a bite. The crunch was loud enough that two pedestrians turned. Mario watched his face like it was a launch window.

"Good right?!"

Alistair took a careful bite, chewed, and said, with the exact cadence of a man filing a report: "It's... very sweet." He kept eating anyway, because refusing a lord's snack was not something a sworn protector did in public.

*WAH! A steward who describes his first foreign meal as "very sweet" and keeps eating out of duty. This is the kind of witness detail that makes me trust a paper. Which makes it worse that I trusted it only for one paragraph, because the paper was about to become a different paper entirely.*

Then Darian said, "So. About going home."

Mario's enthusiasm wobbled. "Oh... uh..." He scratched his head. Then his eyes lit up with the specific brightness that precedes an extremely bad idea. "Wait! Maybe Nintendo has a portal or something!"

Alistair gave him a look. The kind of look that had, in a colder century, preceded duels.

## Part Six: The Phone Call and the Proof

Mario pulled out a small black rectangle, held it to his ear, and announced, "Okay! First step—call Shigeru Miyamoto!"

The name meant nothing to Darian or Alistair. The small black rectangle, on the other hand, meant something to both of them, and neither of them was ready to say what.

The line rang twice. Then a deep voice came through: "MARIO?!"

Mario straightened. "Mr. Miyamoto! We have a situation!"

There was a pause. "What kind of situation, Mario?"

"We got... uh... noble visitors from another world? And they need to go home?"

The static held for a long moment. Alistair held his breath. Darian held his churro.

"Another world," Darian repeated to his steward, in the tone of a man confirming a rumor in front of the person who started it. "Quickly. Go grab something from this world. To prove we went here."

Alistair moved before the sentence finished. A vendor's rack yielded a glitter-lettered Hollywood t-shirt. The pavement yielded a dropped movie ticket stub. A trash bin's edge yielded a soda can, still cold. He was back in seventeen seconds with all three, plus the churro stick he had saved, which he was not going to explain.

The vendor was yelling. Alistair did not look back.

Mario watched the whole thing, phone still at his ear, and said, with genuine admiration: "You two are going to fit in great here."

## Part Seven: The Tablet, and the Article I Wrote

Miyamoto was still talking when Mario put the call on hold. The studio's research wing had been summoned; the scientists would be there in twenty minutes. That left one small window, and Darian used it.

He drew out [[prop:prop_wario_inc_tablet|a slate of black glass]] — *Wario Inc.*, lit across the top in purple — and the screen came up glowing.

"I pulled this up," he said. "There might have been a Mario in our world. In our stories."

Mario's eyebrows climbed. "Wait... there *was* a Mario where you're from?!"

From the phone, Miyamoto's voice sharpened. "What did he look like?"

Darian turned the tablet so both of them could see. And on that tablet, in my own words, was the whole impossible biography: the most famous hero in the Mushroom Kingdom; the man who saved Peach so many times that his name became a verb; the disappearance after eighty-five years of silence; Luigi finding him at the Star Fountain; the flight on wing caps; *nothing can hurt us as long as we're together*; and then gone again, with Luigi at Raventree Manor and a vacuum cleaner and no explanations.

Mario read it standing. He read it sitting. Then the phone slipped out of his hand and hit the pavement with a *thud*, and the street went silent. Miyamoto's voice kept talking from the ground: "—Mario? Mario, what happened—"

Nobody listened.

Alistair read over Darian's shoulder and went pale. "Milord... he was legendary..."

A single tear crossed Mario's cheek. He did not wipe it.

*WAH! He learned his own tragedy from my article. My article. The man is crying about a life I documented, and I cannot decide whether that is the most flattering thing that has ever happened to my filing or the most damning. I do not get to feel flattered about it. Because what I documented was wrong in at least one place, and I found out from a stranger's tears.*

## Part Eight: A Single Question on Hollywood Boulevard

Mario made a small, wounded sound and dropped to his knees on Hollywood Boulevard. A woman stopped. A street performer stopped mid-note. The block seemed to lean in.

"Are you alright?" Darian asked.

Mario shook his head, tears coming faster. "No..."

Alistair put a hand on his shoulder, clearly unsure whether a sworn protector had standing to comfort a crying man from another world.

Darian looked at the tablet, then at Mario, then at Alistair. And then he said the thing that split the whole evening in half:

"Well. If there are TWO of you... then maybe... maybe there are TWO."

Mario's tear-stained face snapped up.

The phone crackled. "What is it, Mario?" Miyamoto again, patient, waiting.

Mario scrambled for the phone with shaking hands. Then he stopped, wiped his face, and looked at Darian like a man asking a question he was afraid to hear back.

"What is your full name?" Darian said. "Are YOU the Mario who disappeared?"

A silence. Mario looked at the pavement. "Mario... Mario Mario?"

Miyamoto, calm through the speaker: "His legal name is just 'Mario.' We didn't give him one beyond that."

Darian turned to his steward. "What was OUR Mario's name?"

Alistair straightened, and recited from memory, which is the only way Alistair ever recites anything:

"'Sir Mario of the Mushroom Kingdom, First Hero of the Plumber's Guild, Defender against Bowserian Forces—'"

The crowd murmured. Somebody whispered, "That sounds like a video game character," and got shushed by three people at once.

"'—Lord Protector of the Toadstool Throne, Bearer of the Golden Fire Flower, Vanquisher of Dark Fountains—'"

Miyamoto cut in, excited now: "That's exactly our Mario! Those are all his titles from our games!"

"'—The Last Champion...'" Alistair finished, and let the rest sit there. "'...before he vanished in 955 BF.'"

Nobody cheered. The street performer played a minor chord, entirely unprompted, and then stopped again.

## Part Nine: A Brother, a Pizza, and a Living Peach

Darian studied the two Marios — the one on the ground in the red cap, and the one standing in his own memory — and asked the question that would make the evening stranger.

"What about this world? If this world is like yours, and you're both Mario, what about other things? Do you have a brother?"

Mario nodded, eager, grateful for a normal question. "Oh! Yeah! I have Luigi!"

He pointed down the street. A man in a green cap was stepping out of a diner, carrying two pizza boxes.

"We both love jumping! We both fight Bowser!" Mario said. "And Peach is our princess here, too!"

Miyamoto's voice came through the phone: "Their stories match perfectly. Even down to minor details."

Darian did not blink. "Peach is still alive here?"

Mario's face lit up, relieved at last. "Oh yeah! Peach is totally alive here! She's in there right now, probably playing some new game!"

Miyamoto added, with the pride of a man who had kept a promise for a long time: "We kept her safe. No assassinations happened here."

Luigi arrived with the pizza, oblivious, and said, "Hey, guys! Got extra pepperoni!"

Alistair took a slice and kept looking between this cheerful Luigi — who still had a brother — and the memory of a Luigi somewhere else, alone in a manor with a ghost machine.

*WAH! Read that exchange again. "We kept her safe. No assassinations happened here." That is a boast. And a boast is the closest thing to a confession a corporation can make. They kept someone safe that I have on record as dead. Either they are lying, or my record is, or the word "safe" means something different out there. I had the whole clipping and I let that sentence pass me like a bus.*

## Part Ten: The Portal That Wasn't

Dr. Takeda's team arrived in lab coats with equipment that hummed. They examined the tablet, then the shirt, the ticket stub, the soda can, the churro stick, and took painless little samples while Mario narrated the whole thing like a nature documentary.

"Are you ready to try something that might send you home?" Dr. Takeda asked.

"My people need me," Darian said. "Yes."

The scanner hummed, turned blue, and bled a single loud *BEEP*. Dr. Takeda's eyes went wide. "It's working!"

Mario jumped up. "YES! Operation: Send Darian Home is a go!"

A second machine wheeled in, bigger, and began to glow — swirling color like the inside of a soap bubble. "The scanner found dimensional resonance," Dr. Takeda said. "A stable path. The rift will only stay open for sixty seconds. You must step through NOW."

Mario grabbed Darian's hand. "Good luck, Lord Darian!"

Luigi bowed. "Safe travels, milord!"

Alistair gave Darian one last nod. They took a breath together and stepped forward, into warm light, into the smell of sunlight, and the team watched them dissolve —

— and then they blinked, and they were still standing in the studio. The machine had gone red. Every monitor read *PORTAL FAILED*. Dr. Takeda slammed a fist on the console. "No! The dimensional resonance must have been unstable!"

Mario's face fell. Luigi stared at where they had been. Nobody had moved two feet.

Darian looked at the red lights, then at the crying-perhaps-not-crying host, and said the most reasonable thing anyone said all night: "Well, I suppose we can stay a few more days while you get this in order?"

Mario brightened instantly. "YES! Of course!" He grabbed Darian's shoulders. "This means we get more time together!"

Alistair exhaled, very quietly. "Indeed, milord. We have time."

*WAH! There it is. The whole ending. The newspaper reported a successful return, with charms and waving and a beautiful goodbye — and the account says the machine never opened at all. A sixty-second portal, a step into light, and a red screen. The paper sold the goodbye. The technology failed. I filed the farewell and never once asked what the machine did afterward. That is the entire mistake in one sentence.*

## Part Eleven: Two Zones, One Studio

Days passed. The scientists recalibrated. Darian and Alistair toured.

The Mario Zone was bright — reds and blues, Toad statues everywhere, a news desk with consoles, and a closet of fifty hats arranged like evidence.

The Wario Zone was a different country. Purple and gold, garish decor, and through the walls came the unmistakable sound of someone shouting, "AND THE CROWN GOES TO WARIOOOO!" followed by obnoxious applause.

Mario rolled his eyes. "Oh... yeah, he has his own show. It's called 'WarioWare!' It's kinda funny but also really weird. He tries SO hard to be as famous as me. It never works."

Luigi laughed. "Never a dull moment with him around."

Back in the Mario Zone, they watched rough footage: a younger Mario hosting, blocky graphics, and then — on the screen — a green-capped Luigi running through Peach's Castle alone, looking panicked.

Mario pointed. "And here we see Luigi having an adventure all by himself! Isn't that neat?"

Beside them, the real Luigi smiled, proud of his on-screen self, completely unaware of what the next tape was about to do.

## Part Twelve: The Tape With One Date on It

On a shelf under the monitors, Darian found [[prop:prop_tape_955_bf|a single tape]]. It had no title. It had one date: **955 BF**.

He held it up. Mario squinted. "That's... weird. This must be from Nintendo Mania's fictional timeline." Luigi frowned. "Wait... that episode doesn't exist yet."

Mario picked up the tape and turned it over, and the look on his face was the first time all week he had looked like a man who worked here rather than a man who hosted here. "We haven't made anything with that date."

Darian slotted it in.

The machine clicked. The screen flickered. And the studio's cheery set vanished behind black-and-white footage: a grainy castle hallway, and then a funeral procession. Mourners in the style of a world they had never seen. A casket draped in purple and gold. Peach's colors.

Everyone gasped.

Darian leaned in. "Look closely."

At the edge of the frame, for one second, stood a shadowy figure in a black cape — half his face lost in darkness, a glint of metal in his hand.

Mario slammed the pause button. The screen froze on the figure. "This... this isn't one of our shows..."

"Pause the video right now!" Darian said, too late, because Mario had already paused it.

The studio went dead quiet. Then every monitor on the set *beeped*, once, together.

## Part Thirteen: A Question Mark in a Circle

The monitors switched as one to a new picture: Luigi struggling in dark water. Bubbles rising. His green cap floating away.

Mario screamed. "NO! TURN IT OFF!"

Luigi fell backward, pale, staring at his own drowning.

The footage played in silence. No music. No explanation. Just the water, the bubbles, the cap, and then — across every screen at once — a single symbol: a black question mark inside a circle.

The tape *shot* out of the player on its own, clattered to the floor, and kept playing on the tiles. Dr. Takeda ran in with two scientists, picked it up, and turned it over. "This... isn't possible."

The label was blank now. Just plastic.

The lights flickered once, twice, and went out for three seconds.

When they came back, Luigi was gone.

The chair where he had been sitting was empty. No note. No struggle. No sound. Mario spun in a full circle, calling his name, his voice cracking. The security feed showed nothing. Dr. Takeda was already shouting about energy readings and missing footage.

Mario grabbed a flashlight and ran for the doors, and the doors had the decency not to stop him — which, given what was coming, was the worst thing they could have done.

## Part Fourteen: The Piece Waluigi Missed

Alistair stood very still in the middle of the chaos and looked at Darian. The scientists were shouting about cameras. Mario's abandoned pizza sat on a desk. And in Alistair's hand, the little Nintendo charm Luigi had pressed on them earlier was glowing — softly, like a heartbeat.

"There seems to be more to this place than we have seen," Darian said. "We should investigate. Are we really in another world, steward?" He lowered his voice. "Who is to say this is not ALSO part of the Doughnut World?"

Alistair's eyes widened. "Milord... you may be right."

They counted it off on their fingers, the way archivists and stewards do when neither wants to say the sentence out loud:

One: the Mario and Luigi here behaved differently from the versions in their own records, right up until they suddenly behaved exactly the same.

Two: the tape should not exist in any timeline, in any world, in any layer.

Three: the reality had *glitched* — a machine that rejected a TV screen, a question mark that owned the broadcast, a security camera that turned toward two guests without being touched.

"What if," Darian said slowly, "they are alternative versions of each other, but they still exist. Both of them."

Alistair considered it. "So... both exist simultaneously?"

"If they are both real," Darian said, "then what took Luigi just now was a third force. Something that is not either Mario." He pulled out his Walupedia tablet and searched: *Mario — Alternate Versions*.

The results loaded. Multiple timelines. Some where he disappeared permanently; some where he stayed the hero. And then, at the bottom, a section titled **Fallen Maris** with one entry: *955 BF — The Disappeared Hero*.

Darian read Waluigi's entry out loud, so that Alistair would hear the words in a voice rather than read them in a screen:

"'This record begins with the tragedy of 955 BF—not when Peach died, but when Mario vanished without explanation. No body found. No note left. Just... gone. Luigi never recovered after this day. He changed completely—became a recluse at Raventree Manor.'"

The tablet screen glitched. A new line appeared that Darian had not searched for:

**WARNING — INCONSISTENT REALITY DETECTED.** The studio lights flickered overhead.

Darian read it again, slower, and then said the quiet part: "This says our Mario disappeared in *955 BF*. But you—all of us—we know Peach died in 955 BF, and the fountain was 1039 BF. This puts the disappearance IN the year of her death. Something is off. Or he just didn't know."

Alistair said nothing. He was watching the dark doorway.

*WAH! He caught the mismatch. A noble from another world, holding a tablet with my own words on it, caught the date error that I had spent a whole morning trying to file around. The clipping placed the disappearance at 955 BF, and I treated it as one more wrong detail in an unverified newspaper. The full account makes it worse, because the account insists on it. Somebody in that world knows the 955 number. Somebody who was not reading my file.*

## Part Fifteen: The Wario Show, and the Head in the TV

The speakers came on by themselves.

*"WELCOME TO THE WARIO SHOW! TODAY'S SPECIAL: TRUTH OR CONSEQUENCES!"*

The voice was distorted, stretched, wrong. Every television on the set went to static, and then to the same picture: a grotesque Wario face, purple lightning crackling behind it, and the face was *grinning*.

Alistair stepped in front of Darian. The furniture began to vibrate.

Then Wario's form started pulling itself out of the screen — limbs stretching, pixels reforming into flesh, his grin too wide, all teeth.

"You want fun?" the voice sang. "I show you fun. No backwards long jump. No time to run."

*"THINK YOU WILL ESCAPE?!"* The voice crashed through the speakers. *"YOU'RE CUCKOO-CRAZY! NOWHERE TO GO BUT STRAIGHT TO ME!"*

The doors locked. The scientists screamed. Wario came the rest of the way through the glass with a sound like a VHS tape being eaten, his body half-flesh, half-glitch.

"We have to go, steward. NOW."

They ran. Wario teleported ahead in a burst of purple static, blocking the hallway, planted like a thumb.

"Wrong!" he sang. "I'm the STAR now!"

Alistair scanned the corridor: a fire axe on the wall, a janitor's cart, a door marked RESTRICTED. "Milord," he said, "I am meant to guide you, but it appears you are doing all the guiding here."

"You're right," Darian said. "So guide."

Wario's body dissolved into the wall and reformed in front of them, and the whole corridor leaned. Darian ran. Wario sang after him, each line landing a half-step ahead:

> Fate is maligned now,
> Deaf to your cries!
> Yes, you will be mine—
> **It's Wario time!**

Alistair caught his lord's arm and steered them through a door that was not an exit. Behind them, Wario's fingers stretched like claws and caught nothing but air, and the wall burst open into static.

"Be consumed by my design," Wario said, in the voice of a man filing paperwork.

Then he was in the exit doorway, arms spread to fill the frame, and the garlic smell rolled in ahead of him:

> Oh, my stomach is rolling
> With the taste of garlic and human fear!
> You can't leave here!

He reached for them. Alistair grabbed the fire axe off the wall and swung it into the frame of the door instead of the man — the whole doorway glitched sideways, and they were through.

*WAH! The stewards in my archive usually get one scene, one quip, and a funeral. This one got a corridor, a fire axe, and his lord telling him to use his brain. I can only assume the full account kept him alive because the paper would not have sold as well with a dead steward.*

## Part Sixteen: The Song Cycle — Wario's Showtime

The floor buckled. Wario's laughter came from everywhere at once.

> In this place, fun never ends—
> Well, not 'til Wario apprehends!
> You skinny chumps who try to flee,
> But you cannot outrun me!
> **WAAAAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA!**
> **AHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA!**

The floor opened. They fell.

The fall ended the way bad dreams end: with a seat. They were in a studio audience, absurdly colorful, while Wario stood on a game-show set in a host costume, manic grin fixed, purple-and-gold banners reading **WARIO'S SHOWTIME!** all around.

The audience — identical, plastic, polite — cheered on cue.

> Wario number one!
> Wario... the LEGEND!
> WARIO!!!
> I GOTTA WIN!
> Ready for round two?!

The audience chanted it back: "WARIO! WARIO! WARIO!" A countdown clock above the stage read *10 SECONDS TO NEXT ROUND*.

A giant wheel spun down from the ceiling, its faces labeled:

> **PIT OF DESPAIR**
> **LAUGH TRACK TORTURE**
> **REALITY CHECK**

The wheel stopped on *REALITY CHECK*.

Wario's body slumped lifeless behind the podium. His head detached, floated up, and grinned.

> When you see the Wario head,
> The face of greed shall never rest
> Until you're dead!
> *(WAAAA!)*
>
> Greed is good! Greed is good!
> Why not submit to me?
> You'll soon see
> Treasures of which
> You have never, ever, ever dreamed!

The treasures appeared: piles of gold coins that looked like teeth, jewelry made of bone, a throne built from trapped screaming faces. Mario gagged. Alistair's hand went to the mic stand.

The head advanced, and it sang:

> Obey Wario!
> Destroy Mario!
> Give me your soul!
> Give me control!

Darian grabbed his tablet and pressed the only button on it he had never pressed. A *click*. The head sang on:

> Riches you can't fathom,
> In a world that's personalized!
> Every atom shifts before your eyes!
> No use running—
> Fate is coming!
>
> Soon, you'll be another victim
> Of the Wario Apparition!
> Say your prayers!
> Sleep in this nightmare!

The head lunged. And Darian clicked the button again.

A blinding white flash tore through the set. Wario's head *screamed* — a sound like a corrupted file — and recoiled, smoke pouring off him, his grin twisting. The audience NPCs flickered, glitched, and vanished. Alistair picked up the fallen mic stand and held it like a pike.

The head came apart pixel by pixel. And it kept singing, because Wario always gets the last line:

> You sought treasure
> In a realm defiled!
> You'll forever wander halls capricious—
> EXILED
> From what you know to be real!
> Now you're Wario's meal!
> In your last heartbeat,
> Choose a god—
> And make your appeal!
> **AHAHAHAHAHAHAHAHA!!**
> **...Have a rotten day!**

He *popped*. Purple pixels scattered, and the game show collapsed into ordinary studio walls.

Mario stared. "It... worked?"

Darian clicked the button a third time. A normal flashlight beam came out.

"All it was," he said, "is a flashlight."

Mario's jaw dropped. Then he laughed so hard he had to hold the wall. "You used a FLASHLIGHT to scare off evil Wario?! That's amazing! That's the funniest thing ever!"

*WAH! I want it on the record that the most expensive artifact in that world — a Wario Inc. tablet, purchased over my objection, with a feature list longer than a castle's tax roll — defeated an interdimensional game-show apparition by being a torch. The tablet did nothing. The flashlight won. I have been telling this story all evening and I am still not over it.*

## Part Seventeen: Two Problems, and a Question Mark

The studio settled. The distortion rolled back like tide. Mario wiped his eyes and looked at Darian.

"Well... what was all that about?"

"I don't know," Mario admitted. "That wasn't normal for Wario. Not at all. Maybe a virus? Something in the system?"

Dr. Takeda approached. "Something in the system, yes—" Mario got between her and the tablet, hands up.

"Right, right—yours, yours!" He backed up protectively. "They're good people! They just love studying weird stuff."

Darian looked at him. "Either way, we still have two big problems: One — Luigi is missing. Two — we need to go home."

Mario's face fell. The studio felt heavier, the way rooms do when the words are true.

"And what about Wario?" Darian asked. "Will he return?"

Dr. Takeda shook her head. "We've never seen anything like that. If it was a virus or a glitch... it might come back."

Mario made a decision with his jaw. "First we find Luigi. THEN we fix the portal machine."

Darian pointed at the television. "Lets head back to the TV. That is square one."

The screen was black. Mario pressed the power button. A normal *No Signal* message appeared. Dr. Takeda checked the settings. "Everything looks reset to factory mode."

"Put in a tape," Darian said. Alistair slid a blank tape into the player.

The screen flickered once. Static snow. Then the machine whirred, and *Super Mario 64* gameplay started — Peach's Castle, perfect controls, nobody piloting it.

The on-screen Luigi ran through familiar rooms. Dr. Takeda leaned in. "This must be saved gameplay data..."

And then the on-screen Mario turned to face the camera, and spoke in a voice they all recognized but none of them wanted to hear.

"Hm..? You looking for someone? Seems you don't-a recognize me. It's-a me..."

Mario — the real one — stumbled backwards. "That's my voice! But that's NOT me!"

The on-screen Mario smiled warmly. "Long time no see, buddy!"

Darian said nothing. Alistair's grip tightened on the mic stand.

"Almost. Aw, you four seem a bit-a scared... Well, don't be." The smile did not move but the voice did. "I'm-a not-a gonna kill you... *yet.* I want to have some fun with you four midgets before I end your lives."

The sprite glitched, grew, reddened. Real Mario screamed: "That's NOT ME! That thing is evil!"

The screen cracked from the inside, and the thing on the other side of it stopped pretending to be a game.

## Part Eighteen: The Mario Who Came Out of the Television

Dr. Takeda slammed the emergency button. Nothing happened. The tape would not eject.

"Oh, don't-a bother using your remote," the voice said. "They're useless here. This is... **MY World.**"

Darian took a step back. Alistair took a step forward. The wall behind them was still ordinary, for now.

"Oh-ho-ho. You're gonna pay for what that traitor of a man you call a father did to me... all those years ago."

Real Mario's face went slack. "My father? I—I never had a dad!"

The voice went on, smooth and patient now, which was worse: "You, Mario, on the other hand... I've-a heard so many stories about you. You've defeated lots of creatures—some like myself. Monsters... Demons... Angels... Freaks..."

The sprite was taller now, edges pixelated, eyes red. "So how's-about we make a deal: Beat me, and I'll-a let you go. Lose... and you perish by my hand."

The room was very quiet. Dr. Takeda whispered, "It's... challenging him to a battle?"

Real Mario swallowed, looked at Darian, then back at the screen. "I have to try..."

"Very well..." The TV vibrated. The pixels swirled. "**Let's-a-go!**"

The screen exploded with light. The evil Mario *leapt out of the television* — taller than normal, pixelated at the edges, red eyes burning — and landed on the studio floor in a shower of static. Real Mario dropped into a stance. Dr. Takeda screamed for everyone to get back.

Darian ran.

Behind him, the two Marios met in the middle of the set: explosions of light, the crash of knocked-over monitors, one voice yelling and one voice laughing in the same tone.

## Part Nineteen: The Steward's Plan and the Camera That Lied

Darian sprinted down the corridor. Alistair kept pace, face pale. Emergency exits glowed ahead — and Darian skidded to a halt.

"No. Wait. I remember this. Don't go to the exit."

"Correct," Alistair said. "We did this with the door. This place uses familiar exits as traps."

They swerved into the employee break room: a couch, a coffee machine with a pot still warm, and a wall of security monitors.

"What is the plan, steward?" Darian said. "You are meant to guide me, but it looks like I'm doing all the guiding here."

Alistair straightened, composure returning. "You're right, milord. I should be leading." He scanned the monitors. "We need to find Luigi. And a safe place to wait out the battle. The break room has the cameras—"

"Then break room it is," Darian said. "The other two options were just cornering ourselves."

Four monitors showed different parts of the studio. One showed the battle — evil Mario pinning real Mario to the floor, purple energy crackling around his fists.

And on [[prop:prop_studio_security_footage|Camera Three]], near the prop room, a figure in green and blue was hiding behind crates. Green cap. Blue overalls. Terrified but unharmed.

"No, no, no," Darian said. "That is NOT Luigi. Look closer."

Alistair leaned in. The figure's hat was the wrong shade. Too tall. Too still. And its edges — he would swear to it later — flickered, once, like a screen losing signal.

The figure turned its head sharply. Where Luigi's face should have been, there were two hollow black eyes.

Neither of them was in the same room as that camera. The one in the room reached through the monitor and waited.

"That thing isn't him," Alistair said, and put his hand on Darian's arm. "Don't go there."

The three remaining monitors went to static. All four — together, in sequence — showed the black question mark inside the circle.

Then the coffee machine went cold.

*WAH! So: the report on the front page that morning — the one I filed, the one with the souvenirs and the handsome farewell — ends with a portal. The full account ends with a camera watching two people through a monitor, a missing brother, an evil version of the most famous hero in the world, and a question mark that keeps showing up at every bad turn like a signature. I did not file a newspaper this morning. I filed a trailer. The archive has been quoting a trailer all day. WAH.*

aftermath:
Standing as of 5 Aethel, 1040 BF — per the full account, not the newspaper.

- The portal machine never opened. Darian and Alistair remained in the Hollywood studio, the devices red, Dr. Takeda promising recalibration over days.
- Luigi was reported missing from the studio after the unsupervised tape played. No note, no struggle, no usable security footage.
- A hostile figure calling itself a version of Mario emerged from a television, challenged the host to beat it or perish, and engaged him on the set. Its fate is unreported.
- The Wario Apparition, which seized the studio systems and ran a game-show segment, dissolved after a Wario Inc. tablet was used as a flashlight. The tablet still works. Waluigi is not sorry.
- The 955 BF tape, the funeral footage, the drowning image and the question-mark cipher remain unaccounted for.
- Darian, Alistair, Mario and Dr. Takeda remain the account's only sources. No publisher, no original film and no independent witness has been produced.

name: The Belly of the Beast
title: The Belly of the Beast: Human Blood Under the Scarecrow, a Door Burned Shut, and the Skittering Grove Inside the Tree
date: 30 Harvestide, 1040 BF — continuing the same storm-night, from the grove into the tree
era: Harvestide 1040 BF — Shadow Estate storm chain
location: The overgrown grove beyond Tymnas's cottage, and the Skittering Grove inside the Scorncrow's tree (Shadowfell)
type: Session Event / Grove Skirmish / Descent
status: Unresolved — the party is inside the Skittering Grove, the jaws are shut, the exit Archie made is sealed, Remi is webbed and separated, and there are Legion soldiers in there with them
summary: The Scorncrow put Feyward Dan down with a murder of crows, Archie slammed it out of the air onto Remi, and Remi — pinned at point-blank range — fired a musket into its face and found human blood. The thing fled into the mouth of its own tree; the party followed, Archie sealed the only exit burning it, Markop pried the jaws open and rigged a rope, and five of them descended into the Skittering Grove: a web-canopied grove inside the tree, hung with wrapped bodies, full of ettercaps, giant green spiders, and Legion soldiers.
description:
*Waluigi has filed three engagements against the Scorncrow. In every one of them the thing shouted that it was not a monster and Waluigi wrote that down as villain theatre, because that is what it sounds like. On the night of 30 Harvestide a fourteen-year-old girl pinned under its body pressed a musket to its face and fired, and the face came off, and the blood underneath was human. This article is partly a correction. WAH!*

The battle continued out of the grove skirmish without a pause. Crows took Feyward Dan down unconscious at Archie's feet; Salam crossed open ground to stabilise him; Archie planted his staff and shook the earth, and the Scorncrow's crows simply lifted it off the ground that was failing. It offered a swing — pointed, spiked — and Archie answered by slamming it out of the air knowing full well it would land on Remi. It did. She shot it in the face at zero range.

Wario cleared the shadow servants, freed his motorbike, and rode at everything. The Scorncrow laughed and jumped into the mouth of its own tree. Then the plans came apart: Archie argued for withdrawal and immediately talked himself into arson, Remi honked a horn that laughed in Wario's voice across a fifty-mile radius, Feyward Dan healed himself with every point of magic he owned and reported — inside an insult — that they had not seen half the Scorncrow's power.

Wario rode into the mouth. Remi went in after. Both ended up in cobwebs with the motorbike gone. Archie, outside and unanswered, poured every reserve he had into one weakened fire cast until his eyes turned to fire, and killed the tree, and sealed the exit doing it. Markop pulled a piece of bark and the jaws shut. Then he pried them open again, found a pit, tested it with a torch — and the pit answered, in voices, saying someone was going to burn them all down.

They set a marching order with reasons attached, went down Markop's rope, and arrived in the Skittering Grove.
imageCaption: The mask in flight. Knocked off at point-blank range, it tumbles away trailing straw — and underneath is an ordinary human face. Three filings called this thing a monster on its own denial; this is the moment the denial was tested.

sections.name: I. The Crows Take Feyward Dan
sections.overview:
The crows came off the branches all at once, and the sound they made was not a caw. It was a dry, leathery clatter, a thousand playing cards shuffled at speed, and it went up into the dark and then bent sideways and came down on Feyward Dan.

He got one arm up. That was all the time there was. The mass closed over his red cap and his mail and the shape of him disappeared into a churn of black wings and small hooking beaks, and the noise from inside it was the noise of hail on a tin roof — beaks on steel, over and over, working the gaps in the rings.

"GET OFF —" he said, and then he stopped saying anything.

The birds lifted. They went up in a single spiral, unhurried, the way smoke leaves a chimney, and Feyward Dan came down on his face in the churned mud at Archie Miser's boots. A feather turned over in the air above him and took a long time to land. One of his gauntlets had come off. His fingers moved once and did not move again.

Archie did not look down at him for long. He looked across the grove, at the tall ragged thing standing in the middle of it with straw at its cuffs, and he shouted over his shoulder without turning his head.

"SALAM."

Salam was behind a fallen trunk forty feet back with his hands flat on the wood. He looked at Dan. He looked at the scarecrow. He looked at the forty feet of open churned ground between the two, and he did the arithmetic out loud in a voice that had gone up half an octave.

"Alright — but keep that thing distracted. It's kinda scary."

Then he came over the trunk. He ran badly, low and hunched with his arms tucked, mushroom cap bobbing, the way people run when they expect the sky to be the thing that kills them. He dropped onto his knees in the mud so hard he skidded, and he got both hands under Dan's shoulder and rolled him over out of the wet.

*"Your service won't go in vain,"* Salam said — to a man who was still breathing, which is either the wrong thing to say or the truest thing anyone said all night — and got to work.
sections.waluigi_note: Read the target selection, because it is the whole night in one move. Three engagements this squad has fought, and the Scorncrow opened the fourth by removing the healer before it touched anybody else. That is not a swarm finding a body. That is something that has watched them fight and knows which one to take off the board first.

sections.name: II. Something Really Risky
sections.overview:
"I'm doing something really risky," Archie announced.

Nobody had time to ask which part. He was already running — cloak snapping, boots throwing up wet leaf-litter, the third eye on his forehead wide open and fixed on the scarecrow. Ten paces out he stopped dead, reversed the staff in both hands, and drove it into the earth like a man setting a fence post.

The ground answered. It went first with a deep grinding sound, felt in the teeth before it was heard, and then the whole floor of the grove humped and split. Roots tore up out of the soil, pale and wet. Stones stood on end. The dead leaves jumped an inch off the ground and came down again in a wave that travelled outward from the staff and broke against the tree.

The Scorncrow watched all this happen. Then it laughed — a wet, comfortable sound, like a boot pulling out of mud.

*"Oh, you little thing."*

And the crows came in under its arms. They took it up off the buckling earth, a dozen of them at each shoulder, and it hung there in the air with its heels a foot clear of everything Archie had just broken, tattered coat-tails swinging gently over ground that was still shaking itself apart underneath.

Then it tipped its sacking head to one side, the way you do when you are being polite to a child.

"Care for a swing?"

Above Remi, a branch turned. It came down out of the canopy on a slow creaking arc, thick as a man's thigh, and the end of it was not blunt — it had been split lengthwise into a point, four feet of pale splintered wood, and it was descending exactly where a person's chest would be.

Archie did not shout a warning and he did not dodge. He ran three steps, jumped, and hit the Scorncrow with his shoulder and all of his weight.

He knew, leaving the ground, where the thing was going to land. Remi was standing right there. He could see her. He connected anyway.
sections.waluigi_note: Archie keeps attacking the Scorncrow's relationship with the ground, and the Scorncrow keeps proving it does not have one. Twice now he has broken the earth under a thing that is carried. The crows are not decoration and they are not a mood — they are the landing gear, and until somebody grounds the birds, every tremor he casts is an expensive way to redecorate a field.

sections.name: III. Point Blank, and What Was Under the Face
sections.overview:
The Scorncrow went over backwards. It did not fall like a person falls — it folded, slow and wrong, more sailcloth than body, and it came down across Remi Akamatsu and put her flat in the mud underneath it.

"I'll make sure it's worth it," Archie said, to nobody.

Forty feet away, Wario had both fists on the handlebars of the motorbike and one boot braced against the front wheel, hauling. The rear tyre was buried past the axle in wet dirt. The shadow servants came in around him in a loose ring, unhurried, and he did not look up at them once. He kept pulling.

Eager came in on the fallen Scorncrow with the Shadow Blade lit in his fist and brought it down in a flat silver arc — and stopped it, hard, mid-swing, with his whole body twisting to kill the momentum. The tip passed maybe a hand's width over Remi's shoulder. He backed off three steps with the blade held wide and away, breathing through his teeth.

Underneath several hundred pounds of straw and wet coat, Remi took stock.

"Well, I have this monster on top of me. I'd better get him off of me."

"Preferably push him onto the tremor I made earlier," Archie called.

She got a shoulder into it and shoved. Nothing moved. "It's too heavy."

Then she went quiet. When she spoke again it was flat and small and entirely practical, the voice of somebody who has run out of options and found the last one lying on top of her.

*"Wait a minute. I'm at point-blank range."*

She worked the musket up between her chest and the thing's face, pressed the muzzle into the sacking, turned her head away, and fired.

The bang went flat and huge across the grove. Grey powder smoke rolled out sideways. The burlap mask came off the head entire, tumbling away through the smoke trailing straw and one loose thread, and it landed face-up in the mud six feet away with its painted stitched grin pointing at the sky.

**[[prop:prop_scorncrow_unmasking_note|Underneath it was a face. Pale. Sunken. Human. And it was bleeding the way a man bleeds.]]**

Remi lay under it and looked up at it and did not say anything at all.
sections.waluigi_note: Three filings. Three times that thing has stood in a field and shouted *I am not a monster*, and three times Waluigi wrote the word monster in the very next sentence. A fourteen-year-old pinned under its weight tested the claim at a range of zero inches, because it was the only move she had left, and the claim held. The archive was not lied to. The archive was not listening.
sections.imageCaption: What the musket revealed: the burlap mask tumbling away, and a plain, tired, human face beneath it.

sections.name: IV. Wario Clears the Field and the Scorncrow Leaves It
sections.overview:
Wario let go of the motorbike, turned around, and hit the nearest shadow servant so hard it stopped existing. It came apart into a puff of grey ash that hung in the air and drifted. He took the second one on the backswing. Same puff, same drift, ash settling on his shoulder-spikes like grey snow.

"You shadow chumps have nothing on Wario."

Markop came through the rest at a canter with the warhammer swinging low and level, and hooves and hammer between them put the last of the servants down into dust. For a moment the grove held nothing upright but the party and the thing they had spent all night failing to pin.

Then the motorbike came free with a sucking crack, and Wario was on it and moving — full throttle across the churned ground, headlamp swinging wild, straight at the place where Remi and Archie and the unmasked Scorncrow all were.

The Scorncrow got up. It laughed once with its ruined face, turned, and ran three loping strides at the base of the great tree — and the trunk opened for it. A seam split from root to twenty feet up, bark peeling back in long strips, and behind it there was nothing at all. Black, and a smell of wet rot rolling out. The thing went into it head-first and was gone, and the seam ground shut behind it.

The tree had a mouth. Nobody in the grove said anything for a second.

"Thanks for the ride," Archie said to the motorbike that had not arrived yet. Then, more quietly, and more sensibly than anything he would say for the rest of the night: if we can't win this, we run. Dan goes somewhere safe. Where is Green T? *He seems too powerful* — and the giant was not there to ask.

Wario spat. "We can't let him get away." He jabbed a gauntlet at the ground where Dan lay. That toad's poisoned. Look at him — he's *purple*. Send him away.

Then, over the idling engine: "We should go to the belly of the beast, and uproot it."

Remi said it plainer. If the tree has to die, we go inside and kill it from in there.

And Archie — who has never once in the record declined a chance to set something enormous on fire — stopped arguing for the withdrawal.
sections.waluigi_note: Two plans went on the table and they were the same plan in different hats: Wario's uprooting and Remi's arson both required walking into the thing. The third option had already been said out loud, by Archie, thirty seconds earlier, and it was the right one. Nobody voted it down. He simply talked himself out of it, because the alternative involved fire and he is who he is.

sections.name: V. WAHAHAHAH (Fifty Miles)
sections.overview:
They counted heads by torchlight and came up one giant short. No Green T. No note, no shout, no huge footprints leading anywhere — just an absence where the largest thing in the grove had been standing an hour ago.

Archie, surveying a poisoned Toad, an escaped monster and a sealed tree, proposed that they go and celebrate.

"Green T has his own agenda," Wario said, not worried. "Maybe he's helping some other way."

And then Remi, standing beside the idling motorbike, found the horn and pressed it.

**WAHAHAHAH.**

It was not a honk. It was Wario's own laugh, brass-throated and enormous, blasting out of a chrome trumpet on the handlebars at a volume that flattened the grass. It bounced off the tree. It came back off the hills behind the tree. Crows went up out of the canopy in three separate places. The sound rolled away downhill through the dark and kept going for a long time.

"Wow, that's loud," Archie said.

Then he did the arithmetic and his face changed. "Too loud. Fifty mile radius will hear this."

Behind them, in the mud, Feyward Dan sat up.

He had his hands pressed flat to his own chest and a faint white light was going out between his fingers. The peck-wounds closed over as they watched. He got one knee under himself, then the other, and stood up wobbling, and announced at full volume:

"IT'S OKAY ARCHIE, I AM HEALED! I used magic and everything" — and here his voice dropped to almost nothing — *"although I used all of it"* — and came straight back up — "but it's alright, no need to worry!"

Then he turned on Wario and pointed.

"Wow, this guy is going to be a tough fight." He said it grinning, mocking, a paladin who had been unconscious four minutes earlier. "We all should be in this together. You can't handle this on your own." And then, still grinning: **"I don't think that was half his power."**

Wario's answer was to twist the throttle until the engine screamed, put his head down, and ride at the tree. The seam split open ahead of him and the mouth came apart wide.

"NO ONE CHALLENGES WARIO TO A FIGHT AND GETS A-WAY FROM IT!"

The dark took the headlamp, then the engine noise, then all of it.
sections.waluigi_note: *I used all of it* and *that was not half his power* were said by the same Toad, to the same audience, inside the same thirty seconds. One is a report on the party's reserves and the other is a report on the enemy's. Both are catastrophic and both were delivered as a joke, and not one person in that grove changed a single element of the plan.
sections.imageCaption: "No one challenges Wario to a fight and gets a-way from it!" — the motorbike, freed at last, going straight into a mouth that opens to receive it.

sections.name: VI. Cobwebs, and the Wizard Who Sealed the Door
sections.overview:
"Dang," Archie said.

He cupped his hands. "REMI! WARIO! WHERE ARE YOU?"

The grove gave him back nothing — not an echo, not the engine, not a voice. He decided, correctly for once, that this was the tree's fault.

Inside, it was worse than silence. Remi had come down in something soft and yielding that gave under her boots like rotten netting, and when she tried to move her forearm it stayed where it was. Web. Grey cabled stuff, thick as rope in places, strung floor to ceiling in a room with no visible ceiling. The motorbike was not there. Not fallen, not stuck — *gone*, engine and headlamp and all, swallowed somewhere ahead into the dark.

Something came down a strand above her, in stages, with a click at the end of each stage.

"Oh no. Please don't."

It got closer. She tore her arm free with a sound like fabric ripping, went backwards, and the fangs came down where her shoulder had been. Then she was running — badly, in the dark, off-balance — and her boot went through a floor of silk and she pitched forward into the web and stuck fast.

Outside, Archie levelled his staff and put a bolt of fire into the trunk.

It hit with a crack. Bark blackened in a patch the size of a shield and a little smoke curled off it. The tree did not react at all.

He fired again. The same patch went blacker. Nothing else happened.

So the wizard stopped experimenting. He set his feet, planted the staff, and pulled — everything, every reserve he had, weakened as it was in this place, dragged up through his arms and into one cast. The light climbed his sleeves. The third eye blazed. And then his eyes went, both of them, pupils gone, two sockets of open flame throwing shadows up his own face.

The blast hit the trunk and the tree **exploded** inward, fire running up the inside of the seam, and every peeled strip of bark at the mouth curled in on itself and fused into a solid, smoking, welded scar.

The tree died. The door died with it.

"What have you done?" Markop said. "You've destroyed our only entrance."

Archie was already thinking out loud — move the bark over, maybe, or enlarge the tree — while Markop simply took hold of a loose plate of bark at the seam and pulled it away.

The jaws slammed shut.

Somewhere on the other side of them, in the dark, Wario started running.
sections.waluigi_note: Fire bolt: nothing. Second bolt: nothing. Everything he had: the tree dies and the door welds shut. Then Markop pulls one plate of bark and the jaws close harder. Two men, opposite methods, one minute apart, and the opening got smaller both times. Waluigi has stopped thinking of it as a door that is jammed.
sections.imageCaption: Every reserve he had, in one weakened cast, until his eyes turned to fire. The tree died. So did the exit. Markop recoils behind him.

sections.name: VII. Inside: Crows, Webs, and a Guard With a Spear
sections.overview:
What happened inside is a combat log, and Waluigi files it as one, because the people in it did not have the luxury of a story.

The Scorncrow came out of the dark already multiattacking — and it did not go for the man. It went for the machine. **Murder of Crows**, twice, sixteen to hit at disadvantage, feathers boiling out of the black around the motorbike and fourteen points of damage torn out of a thing made of steel. Chrome went. Spokes went. Then it turned on the owner: two more, seventeen and thirteen, and Wario disappeared inside a churning column of wings.

Then **Shadow Jump**, a bonus action, and it simply was not standing there any more.

The grove joined in behind it, and it came in bold. *Ettercap morale: BOLD (84).* Multiattack, and a dash straight at Remi, long limbs moving over the web faster than anything with that many joints should. *Giant Green Spider: BOLD (84)* — a **Web** at a guard, DC 12 Strength, and the man went over sideways with his legs bound to his chest. A second spider rushed the same guard and webbed him again where he lay.

The ettercap broke off Remi and dashed at Wario. Then it changed its mind, spun, and cast **Web Strand** at the guard — DC 12 Dexterity — and **Reeled** him in on the line as a bonus action, hauling a grown man across the floor of the grove on a rope of spit.

Then it went back for Remi and webbed her. Twice.

*Wario retreated from Remi's position.* The log gives no reason but one word: morale.

And the guard — flat on his back, wrapped twice, dragged in on a string, with no name recorded anywhere in this file — got an arm loose, set the spear, and put five points into the ettercap standing over him.

That is the only friendly attack in the entire interior log.
sections.waluigi_note: It attacked the motorbike first. Not the rider — the wheels. Something in that tree identified this party's only means of leaving and destroyed it before laying a claw on the man sitting on it, and then it Shadow Jumped clear before anyone could answer. Waluigi has been filing that thing as a prankster with a scythe. It is a tactician, and it has been taking notes for three engagements.

sections.name: VIII. The Torch Test, and the Voices That Answered It
sections.overview:
Markop got both hands into the welded seam and pulled. Wood shrieked. The jaws came apart maybe four feet and stayed there, quivering, held open on a centaur's shoulders.

Inside was darkness. He put his head into it and looked down, and the darkness kept going — past the roots, past anything a torch could reach, a shaft dropping away into the ground under the grove.

"Anyone have a rope?" Markop asked.

"I don't think soooo," said Dan.

So they [[prop:prop_belly_torch_test|measured it the way you measure a hole]] when you have nothing to measure it with. Somebody lit a torch, leaned over the gap, and dropped it in.

They waited for the sound of it landing. It never came.

*Inside*, though, in the dark, in the webs, Remi heard something else entirely — voices, several of them, close and panicking and talking over each other:

> *"There's a fire —"*
> *"Someone is causing a fire —"*
> *"They're going to burn us all down!"*

And then the torch came back out. Not up through the jaws where it had gone in — it popped out of a split in the *trunk*, six feet to the left, and dropped smoking into the mud at Markop's hooves, still lit.

Nobody outside heard a single word. They looked at the returned torch and read it as a pit being unhelpful.

Then Markop set [[prop:prop_belly_marching_order|the marching order]], and he gave his reasons out loud, which is more than anyone else did all night:

> **Feyward Dan** — paladin. Front.
> **Eager** — scout.
> **Archie** — squishy. Middle.
> **Salam.**
> **Markop** — rear, and the rope is his.

He braced against the trunk, took two turns of hemp around his own barrel, and paid it out hand over hand into the hole. One by one they went down past the bark teeth into the belly of the beast.
sections.waluigi_note: Somebody in that hole said *us*. Not a shriek, not noise — a plural. Whatever is down there can hear a fire, work out that a person caused it, guess what that person intends, and describe itself as a group with a shared fate. The party dropped a torch into a pit to find the bottom and got a coherent objection back, and only one of them was on the right side of the wood to hear it.
sections.imageCaption: The jaws pried open, Markop's rope going down into a pit a thrown torch could not measure, and Remi's torch — the only light anyone brought to it.

sections.name: IX. The Skittering Grove
sections.overview:
Markop's hooves came down on grey earth, and he stopped.

He did not stop the way you stop in a new place. He stopped the way you stop in a room you have been in before and did not expect to be in again — weight going back off the front hooves, head coming up, one long look across the whole span of it before he said anything at all.

"I know this place."

Nobody answered him, because nobody else did.

> At the heart of this skittering grove is a great, towering tree with vast branches reaching out to form a massive canopy over the area. Its boughs are coated in thick webs that are an unnerving mockery of foliage, and hanging from them are the forms of wrapped creatures, both beast and man, dangling like macabre fruit.
>
> This tree is long dead, some terrible malady having killed it from the inside out years ago. Now its dark roots jut from grey earth which no longer nourishes it, as its great arms serve as home to an unimaginable host of creeping, crawling arachnids that accost anything which foolishly wanders into their domain.

There was no sky. That was the first thing. Overhead, where weather should be, there was the ribbed inner wall of a trunk going up and up into green-grey murk — and under it a whole dead forest, standing inside a tree that had been growing in a field an hour ago.

The bundles turned slowly on their threads. Some were the size of a dog. Some were not.

Markop was not looking at the bundles. He walked forward eight or nine paces with the rope still over his shoulder, past the roots, and stopped again at a broad flat stump about four feet across, its top scarred pale where an axe had once gone into it and been pulled back out.

He put a hand flat on it.

This was the Silent Grove. This was the stump they had piled the loot on after they put the Arachnid Matriarch down — the War Mage's Staff that Markop had claimed on Archie's behalf and carried out himself, the Web-Woven Scale, the three healing potions Rodger had grabbed like a man counting his own heartbeats. Same grove. Same tree. Same stump. They had walked out of this place in daylight through open woodland on Raventree Manor's northwestern boundary, and they had just come back into it on a rope, through the jaws of a scarecrow's tree, in the Shadowfell.

"This is the Silent Grove," Markop said. "We cleared it."

Remi loosed an arrow at a spider on a strand and missed, and the shaft went off into the webbing and made no sound landing.

"It seems like I hear someone yelling," she said.

"WHERE ARE YOU!" Markop shouted, and the grove ate it — the same way it had eaten sound the first time, silk taking the edges off every noise until shouting was a thing you did for your own benefit.

Archie stood at the bottom of the rope and thought about spells, which is what a wizard does when he has spent every one of them.

Then Markop found the motorbike. It was lying on its side in the roots at the foot of the great tree, headlamp cracked, chrome dulled with dust, perfectly intact. He stood over it for a while. He is a centaur. There was no arrangement of centaur and motorbike that worked, and both of them knew it.

"If there is a will, there is a way," Archie said, unhelpfully.

Spiders everywhere, on every strand, at every height.

And, in among them, moving in a formation that spiders do not use: **Legion soldiers.**

Remi took stock of the situation and identified the only objective that mattered — figuring out how not to die.
sections.waluigi_note: Markop said *I know this place* and the record should have stopped dead. This is the Silent Grove. Same dead tree, same web canopy, same grey earth, same stump they stacked the loot on the night they banished the Arachnid Matriarch — a place this party cleared, on Raventree Manor's grounds, that you reached by walking. They have just re-entered it by rope, through a scarecrow's mouth, in the Shadowfell. Nobody else recognised it. One centaur with a good memory is the only reason the archive knows the Scorncrow's tree opens onto ground we already own, and Waluigi wants the obvious question printed: if that grove can be somewhere else now, what else that we cleared is still where we left it? And the Legion are standing in it.
sections.imageCaption: The Skittering Grove: webs where foliage should be, wrapped shapes hanging from the boughs like fruit, and Wario's motorbike abandoned in the roots.
